chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXVII
paragraphs:
Let the lofty Muse sing of the gods and their love;
We mortals must sing of the people below.

A distinguished philosopher I know, who can lend dignity even to ugly furniture by bringing it into the calm light of science, once showed me a small but revealing fact. A tall mirror, or a broad sheet of polished steel kept bright by a housemaid, has countless tiny scratches running in every direction. Set a burning candle before it, however, and suddenly those scratches seem to form beautiful concentric circles around that little sun. We can prove that the scratches run impartially every which way: the flattering pattern exists only because the candle lights up a particular selection of them. There is a parable here. The scratches are events; the candle is the self-importance of someone who is not present—Miss Vincy, for instance. Rosamond had her own private Providence. It had kindly made her more attractive than other girls, and now seemed to have arranged Fred’s illness and Mr. Wrench’s mistake so that she and Lydgate could be brought usefully close together. To go away to Stone Court or anywhere else, as her parents wished, would have frustrated these arrangements, especially when Mr. Lydgate himself considered the precaution unnecessary. So, while Miss Morgan and the children were sent to a farmhouse on the morning after Fred’s illness became clear, Rosamond refused to abandon her father and mother.

Her poor mother, indeed, would have moved any human heart. Mr. Vincy, devoted to his wife, was more frightened for her than for Fred. Without his insistence she would never have rested. All her brightness had faded. She no longer noticed the clothes she had always kept so fresh and cheerful; she resembled a sick bird, its eyes dull and feathers ruffled, scarcely registering the sights and sounds that usually interested her most. Fred’s delirium broke her heart: he seemed to be wandering somewhere she could not follow. After her first angry outburst against Mr. Wrench she became very quiet. Her one low appeal was to Lydgate. She would follow him from the room, lay a hand on his arm, and moan, “Save my boy.” Once she begged, “He’s always been good to me, Mr. Lydgate. He’s never spoken harshly to his mother”—as though Fred’s suffering were a charge she must defend him against. The deepest strands of her maternal memory had come alive. This young man, whose voice softened whenever he addressed her, was still the baby she had loved before his birth with a love she had never known before.

“I have every reason to hope, Mrs. Vincy,” Lydgate would tell her. “Come downstairs with me and we’ll discuss his food.” This brought her into the parlor with Rosamond and gave her a change, while he gently surprised her into drinking some tea or broth prepared for her. He and Rosamond were continually cooperating over such things. He nearly always saw her before entering the sickroom, and she asked his advice about helping her mother. She showed admirable composure and skill in acting on his suggestions. It was hardly surprising that the prospect of seeing Rosamond began to blend with his concern for the patient, especially once the crisis had passed and he felt confident that Fred would recover. While the outcome was still uncertain, he had recommended consulting Dr. Sprague, who would have preferred to stay out of the case for Wrench’s sake. After two consultations, though, Lydgate was left in charge, with every reason to give his closest attention. He visited the Vincys morning and evening. Gradually these visits grew cheerful: Fred was now merely weak, needing every possible indulgence and quite aware that he needed it. Mrs. Vincy began to feel that the illness, after all, had turned into a celebration of her motherly tenderness.

Both parents found a further cause for cheer when old Mr. Featherstone sent word through Lydgate that Fred must hurry up and recover: he, Peter Featherstone, could not do without the boy and sorely missed his visits. The old man was becoming confined to bed himself. Mrs. Vincy repeated these messages when Fred was well enough to listen. He turned his fine, shrunken face toward her; his thick fair hair had been cut off, and his eyes looked larger than before. He was longing for news of Mary, wondering how she felt about his illness. He said nothing. But lovers, with their rare understanding, can listen with their eyes, and his mother, in the fullness of her affection, not only guessed his wish but felt willing to make any sacrifice to grant it.
“If only I can see my boy strong again,” she said, foolish with love. “And who knows? Perhaps master of Stone Court! Then he can marry anyone he pleases.”
“Unless she won’t have me, Mother,” Fred answered. Illness had made him like a child, and the words brought tears.
“Here, darling, have a little jelly,” said Mrs. Vincy, privately unable to believe anyone could refuse him.

Whenever her husband was out, she stayed beside Fred. Rosamond consequently found herself alone much more often than usual. Lydgate naturally had no intention of lingering with her, yet their short, impersonal conversations seemed to be producing that peculiar intimacy which takes the form of shyness. They had to look at each other when they spoke, but somehow this ordinary necessity could not remain ordinary. Lydgate began to find the self-consciousness uncomfortable. One day his eyes darted down or anywhere else, like a puppet badly handled. This did not improve matters: next day Rosamond lowered hers, and when their eyes finally met, they were both more embarrassed than ever. Science offered no remedy, and since Lydgate had no wish to flirt, foolishness seemed to offer none either. He was therefore relieved when their neighbors stopped treating the house as a place of quarantine, and his chances of finding Rosamond alone became much fewer.

Yet once two people have shared that embarrassed awareness of each other’s feelings, its effects cannot simply be erased. Polite conversation about the weather begins to sound like an empty contrivance. Ease is difficult to recover without openly acknowledging a mutual attraction—which need not, of course, imply anything serious or profound. Rosamond and Lydgate gracefully found their way back to ease like this, and their conversations grew lively again. Visitors resumed coming and going, music returned to the drawing room, and Mr. Vincy’s extra hospitality as mayor was fully restored. Whenever possible, Lydgate sat beside Rosamond and lingered to hear her play, calling himself her captive while intending all along to remain free. The very absurdity of imagining that he could immediately afford a satisfactory married household seemed protection enough. Playing at being a little in love was pleasant and did not obstruct his more important work. After all, flirtation did not inevitably mean getting burned. Rosamond, meanwhile, had never enjoyed life so much. Someone worth capturing plainly admired her, and she drew no distinction between flirtation and love, whether in herself or anyone else. She seemed to be sailing on a favorable wind directly toward her chosen destination. Much of her attention went to a handsome house in Lowick Gate which she hoped would soon become vacant. Once married, she meant to find tactful ways of dropping all her father’s visitors whom she disliked, and she pictured various arrangements of furniture in that house’s drawing room.

She certainly thought a great deal about Lydgate too. He appeared almost faultless. If he could only read music, so that his rapt response to her playing had been a little less like an emotional elephant’s, and if he had appreciated the fine distinctions of her taste in clothes more accurately, she could hardly have named a failing. What a contrast to young Plymdale or Mr. Caius Larcher! Neither knew any French or could display impressive knowledge of anything except, perhaps, dyeing and the transport business—subjects they were naturally ashamed to bring up. They were Middlemarch gentlemen, proud of their silver-handled whips and satin neckcloths, awkward in company and timid in their jokes. Even Fred surpassed them, possessing at least a university man’s manner and accent. People always listened to Lydgate. He had the easy courtesy of someone conscious of his superiority, and the right clothes seemed to find him through some natural affinity, without his having to think about them. Rosamond felt proud when he entered a room. When he singled her out with a smile, she enjoyed the delicious knowledge that others must envy the attention paid to her. Had Lydgate known how much pride he stirred in her delicate breast, he might have been as pleased as any man, including one entirely ignorant of bodily humors or fibrous tissue. He thought it one of the prettiest feminine traits to worship a man’s distinction without knowing too precisely what it consisted of. But Rosamond was no helpless girl who accidentally gave herself away, her actions clumsily propelled by feeling instead of guided by cautious grace and propriety. Do you suppose her swift plans and private reflections about furniture and society ever showed in her conversation, even with her mother? Quite the reverse. Had she heard of another young woman caught thinking ahead so immodestly, she would have shown the most charming surprise and disapproval, and probably refused to believe it possible. Rosamond never displayed knowledge unsuitable for a young lady. She remained that blend of proper opinions, music, dancing, drawing, graceful correspondence, a private album of copied poetry, and flawless fair beauty that made a woman irresistible to the doomed man of her time. Please do not judge her unfairly. She harbored no wicked schemes and no mean or mercenary intentions. She scarcely thought about money except as a necessity that other people would always supply. She did not habitually invent lies. If her remarks gave no reliable indication of the facts, that was not their purpose: they belonged among her elegant accomplishments and were meant to please. Nature had used many arts in completing Mrs. Lemon’s favorite pupil, whom everyone but Fred agreed to be an exceptional mixture of beauty, intelligence, and sweetness.

Lydgate enjoyed her company more and more. All awkwardness had disappeared. Their eyes now exchanged a delightful influence, and their words carried that abundance of private meaning which can sound rather flat to a third person. Still, there were no private meetings or whispered exchanges that required anyone else to withdraw. They were flirting, in fact, and Lydgate remained confident that this was all they were doing. If a man could not be both in love and sensible, surely he could flirt and keep his judgment? The men of Middlemarch, apart from Mr. Farebrother, were terribly dull. Lydgate cared nothing for business politics or cards, so where else could he find relaxation? The Bulstrodes often invited him, but their daughters were scarcely out of the schoolroom. Mrs. Bulstrode’s innocent reconciliations of religion and worldliness—life’s emptiness and the attractions of cut glass, human righteousness as filthy rags and the merits of fine damask—did not sufficiently lighten her husband’s unvarying gravity. For all its faults, the Vincy household was more agreeable. And it contained Rosamond, as lovely to look at as a half-open pink rose, equipped with accomplishments for a man’s refined enjoyment.

His success with Miss Vincy, however, won him enemies outside medicine as well. One evening he arrived in the drawing room rather late and found several visitors there. The older people had gathered around the card table. Mr. Ned Plymdale, counted among Middlemarch’s desirable husbands though not its great intellects, was alone in conversation with Rosamond. He had brought the latest “Keepsake,” that splendid publication bound in watered silk which then represented modern progress. He felt particularly fortunate to be the first to examine it with her. He lingered over the engraved ladies and gentlemen, with their glossy copperplate cheeks and smiles, praising the comic verses as excellent and the sentimental stories as interesting. Rosamond received his attentions graciously. Ned was satisfied that he had chosen the finest possible offering of art and literature for a courtship—the very thing an agreeable girl would like. He also had reasons, more inward than apparent, for approving his own appearance. A casual observer might have thought his chin was retreating, as though being slowly absorbed back into his face. It certainly made it difficult to fit his satin neckcloths, for which a chin was then a useful support.
“I think the Honorable Mrs. S. resembles you,” Ned said. He held the book open at the enchanting portrait and gazed at it with a rather lovesick air.

“She has a very broad back. She seems to have posed to show it,” Rosamond replied. She meant no satire; she was thinking how red young Plymdale’s hands were and wondering why Lydgate had not arrived. Her fingers went on making tatted lace.
“I didn’t mean she was as lovely as you,” Ned said, daring to turn his eyes from the portrait to its rival.
“I suspect you’re a very practiced flatterer,” Rosamond answered, certain she would have to refuse this young man a second time.

Just then Lydgate arrived. Before he reached Rosamond’s corner, the book was shut. As he settled confidently on her other side, young Plymdale’s jaw dropped like a barometer forecasting unpleasant weather. Rosamond relished both Lydgate’s company and its effect on his rival. She enjoyed making men jealous.
“How late you are!” she said as they shook hands. “Mamma gave up expecting you a little while ago. How is Fred?”
“Much the same—improving, but slowly. I’d like him to go somewhere else, Stone Court, perhaps. Your mother seems to object.”
“Poor dear!” Rosamond said prettily. Then she turned to her other admirer. “You’ll find Fred terribly changed. Through all this illness we’ve looked on Mr. Lydgate as our guardian angel.”
Ned gave a nervous smile. Meanwhile Lydgate pulled the “Keepsake” toward him and opened it. A brief contemptuous laugh escaped him, and he lifted his chin as if marveling at human stupidity.
“What has provoked that irreverent laugh?” asked Rosamond, pleasantly noncommittal.

“I’m trying to decide which is sillier, the pictures or the writing,” Lydgate said with complete assurance. He flicked rapidly through the pages as though he could grasp the whole book at once, displaying his large white hands to excellent advantage, Rosamond thought. “Look at this bridegroom leaving the church. Have you ever seen such a sugary invention, as an Elizabethan might call it? Could even a haberdasher produce that smirk? Yet I’ll guarantee the story describes him as one of the country’s finest gentlemen.”
“You’re so harsh, you frighten me,” said Rosamond, keeping her amusement within proper limits. Unfortunately, young Plymdale had admired this very picture at length, and he rose to its defense.
“Well, plenty of famous people contribute to the ‘Keepsake,’” he said, sounding both offended and uncertain. “I’ve never heard anyone call it silly before.”

“Perhaps I ought to turn on you and call you a barbarian,” Rosamond told Lydgate with a smile. “I suspect you know nothing of Lady Blessington or L. E. L.” She enjoyed those writers herself, but was slow to commit herself to praise and quick to notice the smallest suggestion that Lydgate did not consider something the height of good taste.
“But Sir Walter Scott—surely Mr. Lydgate knows him,” young Plymdale put in, encouraged a little by this advantage.

“I don’t read literature these days,” said Lydgate, closing the book and pushing it aside. “I read so much as a boy that I imagine the supply will last a lifetime. I used to recite Scott’s poems from memory.”
“I’d like to know when you stopped reading,” Rosamond said. “Then I could be certain of knowing something you don’t.”
“Mr. Lydgate would probably say it wasn’t worth knowing,” Ned remarked, deliberately sharp.
“Quite the opposite,” Lydgate replied, apparently untouched, smiling at Rosamond with infuriating confidence. “Anything Miss Vincy could teach me would be worth learning for that reason alone.”
Young Plymdale soon moved away to watch the whist players. He considered Lydgate one of the most conceited and disagreeable men he had ever had the misfortune to encounter.
“How reckless of you!” Rosamond said, secretly delighted. “Didn’t you notice you’d offended him?”
“What—does the book belong to Mr. Plymdale? I’m sorry. That never occurred to me.”
“I’m beginning to believe what you told us when you first came: that you’re a bear who needs lessons from the birds.”
“There’s certainly one bird who may teach me anything she likes. Don’t I listen gladly enough?”

To Rosamond, she and Lydgate were practically engaged. She had long carried the idea that they would eventually be engaged; and, as we know, ideas tend to become solid realities when the necessary materials are available. Lydgate did have an opposing idea: he meant to remain unattached. But his was merely an absence, a shadow thrown by other intentions that could themselves diminish. Circumstances were almost certain to favor Rosamond’s idea. Hers actively shaped events and watched through alert blue eyes. His lay sightless and untroubled, like a jellyfish dissolving without knowing it.

At home that evening he inspected his small glass vessels to see how a process of soaking was progressing, with his scientific interest quite undisturbed. He wrote his daily notes as precisely as ever. The thoughts he found hard to leave were ideal constructions concerning something other than Rosamond’s virtues; primitive tissue was still the beautiful unknown he pursued. He was also beginning to enjoy the growing, half-concealed quarrel between himself and the other doctors. It would probably become more open once Bulstrode announced how the new hospital was to be managed. There were encouraging signs, too, that the impression Lydgate had made elsewhere might compensate for rejection by some of Peacock’s former patients. A few days later, he happened to catch up with Rosamond on the Lowick road. He dismounted and walked beside her until a passing herd had safely gone by. Then a mounted servant stopped him with a request to attend a household of some importance where Peacock had never practiced. It was the second such summons he had received. The servant belonged to Sir James Chettam; the house was Lowick Manor.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXVIII
paragraphs:
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Any season is a good one to return
To your married home, bringing each other joy.

SECOND GENTLEMAN. Quite true.
No date upon the calendar brings ill
To souls that love has joined. Even death
Would be a sweetness, coming like the waves
While they held one another and could see
No life apart.

Mr. and Mrs. Casaubon came home to Lowick Manor from their wedding journey in mid-January. A little snow was falling as they stepped down at the door. Next morning, when Dorothea left her dressing room for the blue-green sitting room we have seen before, the long avenue of lime trees rose from white ground, spreading white branches beneath a dark, unmoving sky. The flat distance seemed to contract into an unbroken whiteness under an equally unbroken low cloud. Even the room’s furniture appeared smaller than on her first visit. The stag in the tapestry looked more ghostly than ever in its spectral blue-green surroundings; the volumes of elegant literature in the bookcase seemed like fixed imitations of books. Dry oak branches flamed brightly above the logs, bringing an incongruous return of warmth and life—much as Dorothea herself did when she entered with the red leather cases of cameos for Celia.

Fresh from dressing, she glowed with the radiance possible only in healthy youth. Her coiled hair and hazel eyes shone like jewels, and her lips were warm with living color. Above the different whiteness of her fur, her white throat rose and fell with her breathing. The fur seemed to curl around her neck and cling to her blue-gray outer dress with a tenderness borrowed from her own nature, an innocent mingling of living warmth and softness that held its beauty beside the crystalline purity of the snow outside. She placed the cameo cases on the table in the bay window and, without noticing, left her hands resting on them. Her attention had already gone to the still white enclosure that bounded everything she could see.

Mr. Casaubon had risen early, complaining of a pounding heart. He was in the library receiving his curate, Mr. Tucker. Celia would come later, as both sister and bridesmaid. In the weeks ahead there would be wedding visits to receive and return, prolonging that transitional period supposed to match a bride’s excited happiness. They would sustain the feeling of being busy without accomplishing anything, like a dream whose dreamer is starting to suspect it. The duties of marriage, which Dorothea had imagined so momentous, seemed to contract along with the furniture and the landscape walled in by white mist. The clear heights where she had expected to walk in perfect understanding with her husband were becoming hard even to imagine. Instead of the delicious peace of resting her soul on someone wholly superior, she experienced anxious effort disturbed by vague foreboding. When would her days of active, devoted wifehood begin, strengthening his life and lifting hers? Perhaps never in the form she had pictured. Yet somehow—somehow they must. Within this union to which she had solemnly pledged her life, duty would arrive with some fresh inspiration and give a new meaning to a wife’s love.

For now, there were only the snow and the low arch of dark mist. There was the suffocating confinement of a lady’s world, where everything was done for her and nobody needed her help. Any connection with the varied, fertile life beyond it had to be painfully maintained as a private vision, instead of reaching her through demands that could give her energy a purpose. “What should I do?” “Whatever you like, my dear.” That exchange summed up her life since she had stopped having morning lessons and practicing foolish rhythms on the piano she hated. Marriage was supposed to direct her toward worthwhile, necessary work. It had not yet released her from a lady’s oppressive freedom, nor even filled her empty hours with the quiet happiness of tenderness freely given. Her vigorous, flourishing youth stood imprisoned in a life whose confinement merged with the cold, colorless, narrowing view, the diminished furniture, the unread books, and the ghostly stag in its pale, fantastic world, fading out of daylight.

For the first few minutes at the window, Dorothea felt only this bleak oppression. Then a sharp memory came to her. She turned away and walked around the room. The hopes and ideas that had filled her on her first visit, nearly three months earlier, survived now only as memories. She judged them as we judge passing things that have already gone. The whole world seemed to have a weaker pulse than hers. Her religious faith was a lonely cry, an attempt to escape a nightmare in which everything withered and shrank away. Each familiar object had lost its magic, as lifeless as a painted transparency with no light behind it. At last her wandering eyes reached the miniatures. Here, finally, something had gained new life and meaning: the portrait of Mr. Casaubon’s aunt Julia, the woman who had made an unhappy marriage, Will Ladislaw’s grandmother. Dorothea could almost believe the delicate face was alive, with its curious, hard-to-read look of determination. Had only her friends considered her marriage unfortunate? Or had Julia herself discovered her mistake, tasting her bitter tears in the merciful privacy of night? What vast distances of experience Dorothea seemed to have traveled since she first saw this portrait! She felt a new companionship with it, as if it could listen and understand her gaze. This was a woman who had encountered difficulty in marriage. Then the colors seemed to deepen; the chin and lips grew fuller; light seemed to stream from the eyes and hair. The face became a man’s, smiling at her with that absorbed attention which tells a woman that even the slightest movement of her eyelids matters and will be noticed. The vivid image warmed Dorothea pleasantly. She found herself smiling. Turning away, she sat and looked up as though once more speaking to someone before her. As she continued thinking, however, the smile faded. At last she spoke aloud.
“Oh, how cruel to say that! How sad—how terrible!”

She sprang up and left the room, hurrying down the corridor, driven by an irresistible wish to see her husband and ask if she could help him. Perhaps Mr. Tucker had gone and Mr. Casaubon was alone in the library. If her husband could be glad to see her, she felt, all the morning’s darkness would disappear.
But at the top of the dark oak staircase she found Celia coming up. Below them, Mr. Brooke and Mr. Casaubon were exchanging greetings and congratulations.

“Dodo!” Celia said in her quiet, clipped way. She kissed her sister, who put both arms around her, and said nothing else. I think each shed a few secret tears before Dorothea hurried downstairs to welcome her uncle.

“No need to ask how you are, my dear,” Mr. Brooke said after kissing her forehead. “Rome has done you good, plainly—happiness, frescoes, antiquities, all that. Very pleasant to have you home. You’re an expert on art now, I suppose? Casaubon looks a little pale, though, as I’ve been telling him. Rather pale. Working hard on holiday is taking things too far. I did too much myself once.” He still held Dorothea’s hand, but turned toward her husband. “Topography, ruins, temples—I thought I’d found a clue. Then I realized where it might lead, with perhaps nothing to show for it. You can go on indefinitely with that sort of thing and get nowhere, you know.”
Dorothea also looked anxiously up at her husband. Perhaps someone seeing him after an absence could detect signs she had missed.

“Nothing to worry about, my dear,” said Mr. Brooke, noticing her expression. “Some English beef and mutton will soon set him right. Looking pale was well enough when he was sitting for that portrait of Aquinas—we received your letter just in time, you know. But Aquinas—wasn’t he a little too subtle? Does anyone actually read him?”
“He is certainly not a writer suited to shallow minds,” Mr. Casaubon replied, meeting these well-timed questions with dignified patience.
“Would you like coffee in your room, Uncle?” Dorothea intervened.
“Yes, and you must go to Celia. She has important news for you. I’ll leave her to tell it.”

With Celia sitting there in an outer dress exactly like her sister’s, the blue-green room looked far more cheerful. She examined the cameos in placid contentment as their conversation moved to other things.
“Do you think Rome is a nice place for a honeymoon?” Celia asked, with the delicate, ready blush that Dorothea was accustomed to seeing for the slightest reason.
“It wouldn’t suit everyone—not you, for instance, darling,” Dorothea answered calmly. Nobody would ever know what she thought of a honeymoon in Rome.

“Mrs. Cadwallader says it’s foolish to travel a long way just after getting married. She says people grow sick to death of each other and can’t even quarrel comfortably, as they could at home. Lady Chettam says she went to Bath.” Celia’s blush kept rising and fading, seeming
“To run back and forth with messages from the heart, like a messenger hurrying on its errands.”
This had to mean more than her usual blushes did.
“Celia, has something happened?” Dorothea asked with all a sister’s warmth. “Is there really important news?”
“It was because you went away, Dodo. That left Sir James with only me to talk to,” said Celia, a mischievous gleam in her eyes.

“I see. It’s what I used to hope for and expect,” Dorothea said, holding her sister’s face between her hands and studying it with some anxiety. Celia’s marriage now seemed a more serious matter than before.
“It only happened three days ago,” Celia said. “Lady Chettam has been very kind.”
“And you’re happy—truly happy?”
“Yes. We’re not marrying just yet, because everything has to be prepared. And I don’t want it to happen too soon. Being engaged is lovely, I think. We’ll have the rest of our lives to be married.”
“I really believe you couldn’t choose a better husband, Kitty,” Dorothea said warmly. “Sir James is a good man, and an honorable one.”
“He’s continued work on the cottages, Dodo. When he comes, he’ll tell you all about them. Will you be pleased to see him?”
“Of course! How could you doubt it?”
“I was only afraid you might be becoming terribly learned,” said Celia. She regarded Mr. Casaubon’s learning as a sort of damp that might eventually soak into anyone nearby.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXIX
paragraphs: I discovered that nobody else’s genius could give me pleasure. My unfortunate paradoxes had exhausted that source of consolation.—GOLDSMITH.

One morning, a few weeks after coming to Lowick, Dorothea—but why should it always be Dorothea? Was hers the only perspective from which to view this marriage? I object to giving all our attention, all our efforts at understanding, to young faces that keep their bloom despite unhappiness. They too will fade and come to know the older, more corrosive sorrows we are helping to ignore. Whatever Celia thought of his blinking eyes and pale moles, however morally distressing Sir James found his lack of muscular shape, Mr. Casaubon possessed a keen inner awareness and a hungry soul like the rest of us. There was nothing extraordinary in his decision to marry. Society approved it and considered it a reason for flowers and garlands. He had decided he must postpone marriage no longer. A man in his position, he reflected, could expect—and should carefully select—a fresh young woman of his own social standing, religious, virtuous, and intelligent. The younger she was, the better: she would be more teachable and obedient. He would settle a generous income on her and overlook nothing that might ensure her happiness. In exchange he would enjoy family life and leave behind a copy of himself, a duty that the sixteenth-century sonnet writers had pressed on men so urgently. Times had changed; no poet was urging Mr. Casaubon to reproduce himself. Nor, for that matter, had he yet managed to produce copies of his key to mythology. Nevertheless, he had always meant to fulfill his duty by marrying. Now the years were slipping rapidly behind him, the world was growing dimmer, and he felt alone. All this seemed reason enough to hurry after domestic pleasures before time carried them beyond his reach as well.

On seeing Dorothea, he believed he had found more than he required. Here might be a true assistant, making it unnecessary to employ a secretary—a resource he had never used and regarded with suspicious dread. He was nervously aware that people expected him to display a powerful intellect. Kindly Providence had supplied precisely the wife he needed. A modest young wife, equipped with her sex’s appreciative but unambitious abilities, would certainly consider her husband’s mind powerful. It could scarcely occur to him to ask whether Providence had been equally attentive to Miss Brooke’s needs in supplying her with Mr. Casaubon. Society never made the absurd demand that a man examine his own capacity to make an attractive girl happy as closely as he examined her capacity to make him happy. As though a man could choose his wife’s husband as well as his wife! As though he must personally provide good looks for his descendants! Dorothea’s enthusiastic acceptance therefore seemed only natural. Mr. Casaubon believed his happiness was about to begin.

His earlier life had given him few anticipations of happiness. To feel intense joy without physical vigor, a person needs an ardent soul. Mr. Casaubon had never been physically vigorous, and his soul was sensitive but lacked ardor. It was too sluggish to soar beyond self-consciousness into passionate delight. It kept fluttering over the marsh where it had hatched, thinking about its wings and never taking flight. His was a pitiable experience that recoiled from pity and dreaded exposure above all else. His proud, narrow sensitivity had too little substance to turn into sympathy. It trembled like a thread in the small currents of self-absorption or, at best, of conscientious concern about himself. He certainly had a conscience. He could practice stern restraint; he was determined to be honorable according to the established code and beyond criticism by any recognized standard. In his behavior he had succeeded. But making his Key to All Mythologies equally unassailable weighed on him like lead. The pamphlets he called his “Parerga,” or supplementary works, tested public opinion and planted little monuments to his progress; their full importance had gone largely unrecognized. He suspected the Archdeacon had not read them. He worried painfully about what Brasenose’s leading minds really thought, and felt bitterly certain that his old acquaintance Carp had written the dismissive review locked in a small drawer of his desk and in a dark cupboard of his verbal memory. Such burdens were hard to resist. They brought the melancholy bitterness that follows excessive claims on the world. Even his religious faith faltered as his confidence in his authorship faltered. Christianity’s promise of immortality seemed to depend on the immortality of the still unwritten Key to All Mythologies. For myself, I feel very sorry for him. Even at best, it is an uncomfortable fate to be highly educated without being able to enjoy anything: to witness the great spectacle of life and never escape a small, hungry, shivering self. Never to surrender to the splendor before us, never to have consciousness joyfully transformed into a vivid thought, a passionate feeling, an energetic deed; always to remain scholarly but uninspired, ambitious but timid, conscientious but unable to see clearly. Becoming a dean, or even a bishop, would scarcely ease Mr. Casaubon’s discomfort, I fear. Some ancient Greek has surely observed that behind the enormous mask and the trumpet that magnifies the voice, our poor little eyes still peer out as usual, and our frightened lips remain more or less anxiously controlled.

Mr. Casaubon had hoped to add happiness and a lovely young bride to this mental estate, surveyed twenty-five years earlier and bounded by such fences of feeling. Yet even before the wedding, as we have seen, a new dejection had come over him: the promised bliss did not make him feel blissful. His inclinations yearned for the easier habits of old. The further he entered married life, the more the sense of performing his duty and behaving correctly outweighed every other satisfaction. Marriage was destined to become another external demand, like religion, learning, and even authorship. Edward Casaubon meant to meet every demand beyond reproach. Even putting Dorothea to work in his study, as he had intended before marrying, took an effort he was always tempted to postpone. Without her persistent appeals, it might never have happened. She had, however, established a routine of coming to the library early to be assigned some reading aloud or copying. The task was easier to define because he now had a specific project: another Parergon, a short monograph on newly discovered evidence about the Egyptian mysteries that would correct certain statements by Warburton. Even this required extensive references, but the sea of them was not quite without shores. Actual sentences would have to be written in the form Brasenose would examine, along with a less intimidating posterity. These small monuments always agitated Mr. Casaubon. Quotations interrupted his digestion; competing argumentative phrases clashed in his head. A Latin dedication was planned from the outset, though nothing about it was settled except that it would not address Carp. Mr. Casaubon bitterly regretted having once dedicated a work to Carp and numbered that specimen of the animal kingdom among the men whose fame would never die. Such a mistake would inevitably make the author ridiculous to the next generation, and might already be making Pike and Tench chuckle in this one.

He was thus going through one of his busiest periods. And, as I began to say a little earlier, Dorothea joined him early in the library, where he had breakfasted by himself. Celia was paying her second visit to Lowick, probably her last before the wedding, and was in the drawing room waiting for Sir James.

Dorothea had learned to recognize her husband’s moods. She could see that the atmosphere had grown foggier in the past hour. She was making her way silently to her desk when he spoke in the remote voice of someone carrying out an unpleasant duty.
“Dorothea, a letter for you came enclosed in one addressed to me.”
The letter covered two pages. She glanced straight at the signature.
“Mr. Ladislaw! Whatever can he have to tell me?” she exclaimed, pleasantly surprised. Then she looked at her husband. “Though I can guess what he’s written to you about.”

“You may read it, if you wish,” Mr. Casaubon said, pointing sternly at the letter with his pen without looking at her. “But I should tell you first that I must refuse his proposal to visit us. I hope I may be forgiven for wanting a period entirely free of the interruptions we have so far been unable to avoid—particularly guests whose restless liveliness makes their company exhausting.”

They had not quarreled since that small eruption in Rome. Its effect on Dorothea had been so lasting that she had found it easier ever since to suppress her feelings than to risk the consequences of expressing them. But this irritable assumption that she wanted visitors who would trouble him, this unnecessary defense against some imagined selfish complaint, stung too sharply for reflection to come before resentment. Dorothea had believed she could be patient with John Milton, but she had never pictured Milton behaving like this. For a moment her husband seemed blindly obtuse and hateful in his injustice. Pity, that newborn child which would eventually master so many storms within her, did not ride the wind on this occasion. Her first words, in a voice that shook him, startled Mr. Casaubon into looking up and meeting her flashing eyes.

“Why assume I want something that would make you uncomfortable? You talk as though I were an opponent you had to resist. At least wait until I show that I’m considering my own pleasure without yours.”
“Dorothea, you’re being impulsive,” Mr. Casaubon answered uneasily.
Clearly this woman was too young to hold the formidable rank of wife—unless she could have been pale and without distinctive features, accepting everything without question.
“I think you were the impulsive one, making false assumptions about my feelings,” Dorothea replied in the same voice. Her anger had not burned out. She thought it ungenerous of him not to apologize.
“Let us leave the subject there, please, Dorothea. I have neither the time nor the strength for arguments of this kind.”

He dipped his pen and made a show of resuming his work, although his hand shook so badly that the writing looked like an unfamiliar alphabet. Some answers turn away anger only by sending it to the far side of the room. To have a discussion calmly dismissed when you feel justice is wholly on your side is even more infuriating in marriage than in philosophy.

Dorothea left both of Ladislaw’s letters unread on her husband’s desk and went to her own place. Scorn and indignation made her reject them, just as we fling away some worthless object when we seem to have been suspected of coveting it. She had no inkling of the complicated roots of her husband’s irritation over the letters. She knew only that they had led him to insult her. She began work immediately. Her hand, unlike his, was steady. Indeed, while copying the quotations he had given her the day before, she felt she was shaping her letters beautifully. The Latin she was beginning to understand seemed clearer in its construction than usual. Her indignation carried a sense of superiority, but for now it found expression in firm pen strokes. It did not become a distinct inward voice calling the once “affable archangel” a poor, inadequate creature.

This apparent peace had lasted half an hour. Dorothea had not lifted her eyes from her desk when a book struck the floor with a loud crash. Turning sharply, she saw Mr. Casaubon on the library steps, bent forward and clinging to them as though in physical distress. She sprang up and reached him in a bound. He was plainly struggling for breath. Jumping onto a stool, she brought herself level with his elbow. All her feelings dissolved into tender fear as she spoke.
“Can you put your weight on me, darling?”

For two or three minutes, endless to her, he could neither move nor speak, but remained there gasping. At last he came down the three steps and sank backward into the large chair she had pulled close to the ladder. The gasping stopped, but he seemed powerless and on the verge of fainting. Dorothea rang the bell fiercely. Soon he had been helped onto the couch. He did not lose consciousness and was gradually recovering when Sir James Chettam entered. Someone in the hall had told him Mr. Casaubon had “had a fit in the library.”

“Good God! Exactly what one might have expected,” Sir James thought at once. Had his prophetic instinct been required to specify the trouble, he felt sure it would have settled on “fits.” He asked the butler, who had brought him the news, whether a doctor had been sent for. The butler had never known his master to need a doctor before. Still, surely they ought to send for a physician?

By the time Sir James reached the library, Mr. Casaubon was capable of a few signs of his usual courtesy. Dorothea, overcome after her first fright, had been kneeling beside him and sobbing. Now she stood and herself suggested that someone ride for medical help.
“I’d advise sending for Lydgate,” said Sir James. “My mother has consulted him and finds him exceptionally capable. She hasn’t thought much of physicians since my father died.”

Dorothea looked to her husband, who silently signaled agreement. They sent for Mr. Lydgate, and he arrived remarkably quickly. The messenger, Sir James’s servant, knew him and encountered him on the Lowick road, leading his horse with Miss Vincy on his arm.

Celia knew nothing of the emergency until Sir James returned to the drawing room and told her. Having heard Dorothea’s account, he no longer called the attack a fit, though he still regarded it as something “of that sort.”

“Poor darling Dodo—how awful!” said Celia, as distressed as her own complete happiness allowed her to be. She clasped her little hands, which Sir James enclosed in his, like a bud held in the generous cup of a flower. “It’s dreadful that Mr. Casaubon should be ill. But I never liked him. And I don’t think he’s nearly fond enough of Dorothea. He ought to be, because I’m sure nobody else would have married him. Do you think anyone would?”
“I always considered it a dreadful sacrifice for your sister,” Sir James replied.
“Yes. But poor Dodo has never done what other people do, and I don’t suppose she ever will.”

“She has a noble spirit,” said the loyal Sir James. The impression had just been renewed when he saw Dorothea slip her gentle arm beneath her husband’s neck and look at him with inexpressible grief. He did not know how much remorse that grief contained.
“Yes,” Celia said. It was all very well for Sir James to say so, she thought, but he would not have been comfortable with Dodo. “Should I go to her? Do you think I could help?”
“Yes, you might go and see her before Lydgate arrives,” Sir James answered generously. “Only don’t be away too long.”

While Celia was gone, he paced the room, recalling his first reaction to Dorothea’s engagement and feeling his old disgust at Mr. Brooke’s indifference return. If Cadwallader—if everyone—had taken the view he had taken, the marriage might have been prevented. It was wrong to let a young girl settle her future blindly like that without trying to save her. Sir James had long stopped regretting anything for himself. His engagement to Celia satisfied his heart. Yet he had a chivalrous nature: surely the selfless service of women had been among the ideals of ancient chivalry? His unreturned love had not soured into bitterness. In dying, it had released a sweet fragrance, memories that lingered around Dorothea and made her sacred to him. He could still be a brotherly friend to her, interpreting her actions with generous trust.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXX
paragraphs: An ill-timed attempt to give someone rest only tires them.—PASCAL.

Mr. Casaubon suffered no further attack as serious as the first. Within a few days he began returning to his ordinary state of health. Lydgate nevertheless seemed to consider the case worth close attention. Besides using his stethoscope, which was not yet a routine instrument in medical practice, he sat quietly beside his patient and observed him. When Mr. Casaubon asked about his condition, Lydgate attributed it to a common fault among intellectual men: working too intensely and with too little variation. The remedy was to accept a moderate amount of work and find different forms of recreation. On one visit Mr. Brooke, who was sitting with them, suggested fishing, as Cadwallader did, or setting up a room with a lathe and making toys, table legs, and similar things.

“In other words, you advise me to bring on my second childhood early,” poor Mr. Casaubon replied with some bitterness. Turning to Lydgate, he added, “I should find these activities about as restful as prisoners find picking apart old rope in a correctional institution.”

“I admit that amusement is a rather inadequate prescription,” said Lydgate, smiling. “It’s rather like telling someone to cheer up. Perhaps I should say you must accept a little boredom instead of continuing to work.”

“Exactly, exactly,” Mr. Brooke said. “Have Dorothea play backgammon with you in the evening. And during the day—shuttlecock! I can’t think of a better game. It used to be all the fashion. Of course, your eyes might not be up to that, Casaubon. Still, you have to relax. You could take up some light branch of study. Shells, for example—I always imagine the study of shells must be light. Or let Dorothea read you something entertaining. Smollett—‘Roderick Random,’ ‘Humphry Clinker.’ A little coarse in places, but now she’s married she can read anything. I remember laughing enormously. There’s a very funny passage about a postilion’s breeches. Nobody writes humor like that now. I’ve been through all these things myself, but they might be fresh to you.”

“As fresh as a diet of thistles” would have expressed Mr. Casaubon’s feelings. Out of respect for his wife’s uncle, however, he merely bowed in resignation and remarked that those books had doubtless “provided occupation for a certain class of intellect.”

“You see, Casaubon has been rather narrow,” the able magistrate told Lydgate once they were outside. “When you stop him doing his particular work, he doesn’t know where to turn. Very deep work, I believe—research and all that. I never let myself fall into that. I’ve always been versatile. A clergyman’s a little hemmed in, though. Now, if they made him a bishop! He wrote a very good pamphlet for Peel. There’d be more activity, more ceremony; he might put on some flesh. But I advise you to talk to Mrs. Casaubon. My niece is clever enough for anything. Tell her he needs liveliness and distraction. Set her thinking of ways to amuse him.”

Lydgate had already decided to speak to Dorothea. She had not been there for her uncle’s cheerful proposals for brightening life at Lowick, but she was usually beside her husband. The unmistakable anxiety in her face and voice whenever his health or feelings were involved made a drama Lydgate was inclined to observe. He told himself it was simply right to explain her husband’s likely future, but he also knew that a confidential conversation with her would interest him. Doctors like studying the mind, and such studies can tempt them into grave predictions that life and death easily overturn. Lydgate had often mocked this habit of needless prophecy. He intended to be cautious now.

He asked for Mrs. Casaubon and learned that she was out walking. As he was leaving, she and Celia appeared, their faces bright from battling the March wind. When he requested a private word, Dorothea opened the nearest door, which happened to be the library’s. At that moment she could think only of what he might say about her husband. She had not entered the room since the attack, and the servant had left the shutters closed. The narrow panes above them still admitted enough light to read.

“I hope you don’t mind the darkness,” Dorothea said, standing in the center of the room. “Since you banned books, we haven’t been using the library. But I hope Mr. Casaubon will soon return to it. Isn’t he improving?”
“Yes, far faster than I first anticipated. In fact, he’s already almost back to his usual health.”
“You aren’t afraid of another attack?” Her quick ear had caught a meaning beneath his tone.

“It’s particularly difficult to predict the course of a case like this,” Lydgate said. “The one thing I can say confidently is that we should take great care to prevent Mr. Casaubon from overtaxing his nervous strength in any way.”

“Please tell me plainly,” Dorothea begged. “I couldn’t bear to think there was something I hadn’t been told, something that would have changed my behavior if I’d known.” The words escaped like a cry, clearly expressing an experience still painfully close to her.
“Do sit down,” she added. She took the nearest chair and removed her bonnet and gloves, instinctively setting formality aside when so much was at stake.

“What you’ve just said confirms my own judgment,” Lydgate answered. “I believe a doctor should prevent regrets of that kind wherever possible. But please understand that your husband’s case is precisely the sort whose outcome is hardest to predict. He might live fifteen years or longer without being much less healthy than he has been until now.”
Dorothea had gone very pale. When he paused, she said quietly, “You mean if we take great care.”
“Yes. He needs protection against emotional disturbance of any kind, and against working too hard.”
“If he had to abandon his work, he’d be utterly unhappy,” she said, seeing that misery in a flash.

“I realize that. All we can do is use every direct and indirect means to make his occupations more varied and less demanding. If circumstances are favorable, as I said, there is no immediate danger from the heart condition I believe caused this attack. But it could develop more quickly. This is one of the conditions in which death can come suddenly. Nothing that might be affected by that possibility should be overlooked.”

For a few moments neither spoke. Dorothea sat as motionless as marble, though inwardly she was so intensely alive that never before had her mind passed over so many scenes and motives in so little time.
“Please help me,” she said at last, still in that low voice. “Tell me how I can help him.”
“Would a journey abroad be possible? You’ve recently been to Rome, haven’t you?”
The memories that made this suggestion utterly hopeless stirred a fresh current of feeling and broke her pale stillness.
“Oh, no, that wouldn’t help. Nothing could be worse,” she said with a more childlike despair, tears running down her face. “Nothing can do any good unless he enjoys it.”
“I wish I could have spared you this suffering,” Lydgate said. He was deeply moved, yet puzzled by her marriage. Women exactly like Dorothea had no place in his received ideas.
“You were right to tell me. I’m grateful you told me the truth.”

“I should make clear that I don’t intend to explain this to Mr. Casaubon himself. I think it best that he know only that he must avoid overwork and follow certain rules. Anxiety, whatever its cause, would be the very worst thing for him.”

Lydgate stood, and Dorothea rose automatically with him, undoing her cloak and throwing it aside as though she could not breathe in it. As he bowed to leave, an impulse that would have become a prayer had she been alone made her speak with a sob in her voice.

“Oh, surely you’re a wise man? You understand life and death. Tell me what to do. Think how I can help. He’s spent his whole life working and looking toward the future. He cares about nothing else. And nothing else matters to me—”

For years Lydgate remembered the effect of that unplanned appeal: one soul calling to another, aware only that their kindred natures moved through the same tangled world, the same troubled life lit by uncertain flashes. Yet what could he say now beyond promising to see Mr. Casaubon again the next day?

After he left, Dorothea burst into tears, releasing the pressure that had seemed to suffocate her. Then she dried her eyes, remembering that she must hide her distress from her husband. Looking around, she thought she must tell the servant to put the room in its usual order, since Mr. Casaubon might want to come in at any time now. Letters still lay untouched on his desk from the morning of his attack. Among them, as she remembered all too well, were Ladislaw’s, including her own unopened letter. Their painful associations had deepened with the sudden illness. She felt that the upset caused by her anger might have helped bring it on. She had not wanted to fetch the letters from the library: there would be time enough to read them when they were forced upon her again. Now, however, she thought they ought to be removed from her husband’s sight. Whatever had irritated him about them, he must be spared another irritation if possible. She first scanned the letter addressed to him, to find out whether a reply was needed to prevent the unwelcome visit.

Will was writing from Rome. He began by saying that he owed Mr. Casaubon so much that any thanks seemed presumptuous. Unless he were grateful, he would be the most contemptible scoundrel ever to find a generous friend. Elaborate expressions of gratitude would amount to announcing, “I’m honest.” But he had come to see that his faults, often pointed out by Mr. Casaubon himself, could be corrected only by a more demanding situation—the necessity his relative’s generosity had so far spared him. If any repayment were possible, he hoped to make the best one by proving the value of the education he owed to Mr. Casaubon and by no longer drawing on money to which others might have a better claim. He was returning to England to seek his fortune, as other young men with nothing but their brains had to do. His friend Naumann had asked him to take charge of the “Dispute,” the painting commissioned for Mr. Casaubon. With his and Mrs. Casaubon’s permission, Will would bring it to Lowick himself. If a visit would be inconvenient, a letter sent within the next fortnight to be held for him at the Paris post office would prevent it. He enclosed a letter to Mrs. Casaubon continuing a conversation about art they had begun in Rome.

Dorothea opened her letter and found a spirited continuation of his objections to her uncompromising sympathy for suffering, and to her lack of a robust, impartial delight in things as they were. It overflowed with youthful energy; just now she could not read it. The other letter required immediate action. There might still be time to keep Will from coming to Lowick. Eventually she gave it to her uncle, who was still in the house, and asked him to explain that Mr. Casaubon had been ill and was not well enough to receive visitors.

Nobody was more willing to write a letter than Mr. Brooke. His only difficulty was keeping it short. On this occasion his ideas spread over three large pages and into the inner folds. All he had said to Dorothea was:

“Of course I’ll write, my dear. A very clever young fellow, this Ladislaw. I expect he’ll make something of himself. A good letter, too—shows he understands things. Well, I’ll tell him about Casaubon.”

But the tip of Mr. Brooke’s pen was an organ of thought in its own right. It produced sentences, particularly kindly ones, before the rest of his mind could catch up. It voiced regrets and suggested solutions which, on rereading, struck him as wonderfully well phrased—surprisingly apt—and led him toward conclusions he had never previously considered. This time the pen thought it such a pity that young Ladislaw should miss coming to the neighborhood just now. Mr. Brooke could have got to know him better, and they could have examined the long-neglected Italian drawings together. The pen also took such an interest in a young man beginning life with a supply of ideas that, by the bottom of the second page, it had persuaded Mr. Brooke to invite Will to Tipton Grange instead of Lowick. Why not? There would be plenty for them to do together. This was a time of exceptional development; the political horizon was widening, and—in short, his pen launched into a little speech it had recently reported for the rather poorly edited “Middlemarch Pioneer.” As he sealed the letter, Mr. Brooke felt pleasantly stirred by a crowd of hazy plans. A young man who could put ideas into shape; the purchase of the “Pioneer” to prepare the way for a new candidate; documents put to use—who could say where it might all lead? Celia would soon be married, and having a young fellow at his table would be agreeable, at least for a while.
He left without telling Dorothea what he had written. She was occupied with her husband, and really these matters were of no concern to her.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXXI
paragraphs:
How can you find the note of that great bell,
Too heavy for your strength? Play a flute
Beneath its finely blended metal. Listen
Until the right note runs out, clear as silver:
Then the enormous bell will stir; its mass,
With countless waves vibrating all together,
Will answer, low and soft, in harmony.
That evening Lydgate told Miss Vincy about Mrs. Casaubon, particularly stressing the depth of feeling she seemed to have for that stiff, scholarly man thirty years her senior.

“Naturally she’s devoted to her husband,” Rosamond replied. To the man of science, the assumption that one thing necessarily followed the other was the most charming a woman could hold. Meanwhile she was thinking that being mistress of Lowick Manor, with a husband who might soon die, was not such a dismal fate. “Do you find her very beautiful?”
“She’s certainly beautiful, though I haven’t given it any thought,” Lydgate said.
“I suppose that wouldn’t be professional,” said Rosamond, showing her dimples. “But how your practice is growing! First the Chettams called you in, didn’t they? And now the Casaubons.”

“Yes,” he answered as if reluctantly conceding the point. “But I actually prefer treating poor people. These wealthy patients offer less variety, and there’s more fuss to endure and more nonsense to listen to respectfully.”
“No more than you hear in Middlemarch,” Rosamond said. “And at least their corridors are spacious and everything smells of rose petals.”

“Quite right, Mademoiselle de Montmorenci,” Lydgate replied. He bent his head slightly toward the table, slipped his ring finger under the delicate handkerchief lying at the opening of her little bag, and lifted it as though to enjoy its perfume, smiling at her all the while.

This pleasant holiday freedom, in which Lydgate hovered about Middlemarch’s finest flower, could not last forever. Social isolation was no more possible there than anywhere else. Two people who kept flirting could hardly escape the various entanglements and burdens, collisions, blows, and movements through which everything makes its way. Anything Miss Vincy did would attract comment. She was perhaps especially visible to admirers and critics now because, after some resistance, Mrs. Vincy had gone with Fred for a short stay at Stone Court. It was the only way to satisfy old Featherstone and at the same time keep watch against Mary Garth, who seemed a less acceptable daughter-in-law with every stage of Fred’s recovery.

Aunt Bulstrode, for instance, visited Lowick Gate rather more often now that Rosamond was alone. She had a proper sisterly feeling for her brother: she always thought he could have married better, but wished his children well. Mrs. Bulstrode and Mrs. Plymdale were old friends. Their tastes in silk, patterns for underclothes, china, and clergymen were much alike. They shared small worries about their health and housekeeping. Mrs. Bulstrode’s various advantages—greater seriousness, more respect for intellect, and a house outside the town—occasionally colored their conversations without disrupting the friendship. Both were well-meaning women who understood little of their own motives.
During a morning call on Mrs. Plymdale, Mrs. Bulstrode happened to say that she must leave to visit poor Rosamond.
“Why ‘poor Rosamond’?” asked Mrs. Plymdale, a sharp little woman with round eyes, rather like a tame falcon.
“She’s so pretty, and she’s been brought up with so little thought. Her mother has always been frivolous, you know. It makes me worry about the children.”

“Well, Harriet, to speak frankly,” Mrs. Plymdale said emphatically, “anyone would expect you and Mr. Bulstrode to be delighted with what has happened. You’ve both done everything possible to advance Mr. Lydgate.”
“What do you mean, Selina?” Mrs. Bulstrode asked, genuinely astonished.

“Not that I’m anything but grateful on Ned’s account,” Mrs. Plymdale went on. “He could certainly afford a wife like that better than some people, but I’d rather he looked elsewhere. Still, a mother worries. Some young men would fall into bad habits over such a disappointment. And if I have to say it, I’ve never been fond of strangers coming into town.”

“I’m not sure about that, Selina,” Mrs. Bulstrode replied, adding a little emphasis of her own. “Mr. Bulstrode was once a stranger here. Abraham and Moses were strangers in the land, and we’re told to welcome strangers. Particularly,” she added after a pause, “when there’s nothing to object to in them.”
“I wasn’t speaking from a religious perspective, Harriet. I was speaking as a mother.”
“Selina, I’m sure you’ve never heard me object to any niece of mine marrying your son.”

“Oh, it’s Miss Vincy’s pride, nothing else,” said Mrs. Plymdale, who had never fully confided in “Harriet” on this subject before. “No young man in Middlemarch was good enough for her. I’ve heard her mother say so. Hardly a Christian attitude, I think. But from what I hear, she’s found someone just as proud as herself.”
“Surely you don’t mean there’s something between Rosamond and Mr. Lydgate?” Mrs. Bulstrode asked, rather embarrassed to discover her own ignorance.
“Can you really not have heard, Harriet?”
“I go out so little, and I dislike gossip. I never hear any, really. You meet so many people I don’t. Your circle is rather different from ours.”
“But your own niece, and your husband’s great favorite—and yours too, Harriet, I’m sure! At one point I thought you had him in mind for Kate, when she’s older.”
“I can’t believe there’s anything serious yet,” said Mrs. Bulstrode. “My brother would certainly have told me.”

“Well, everyone has their own way of doing things. But I understand that nobody can see Miss Vincy with Mr. Lydgate without assuming they’re engaged. Still, it’s no concern of mine. Shall I wrap up the mitten pattern for you?”

Mrs. Bulstrode drove to her niece with a new worry on her mind. She was elegantly dressed herself, but felt rather more regret than usual on seeing that Rosamond, who had just come home and was still in outdoor clothes, had dressed almost as expensively. Mrs. Bulstrode looked like a smaller, female version of her brother, without any of her husband’s subdued pallor. Her eyes had an honest directness, and she did not talk around a subject.

“You’re by yourself, I see, my dear,” she said as they entered the drawing room, looking gravely around. Rosamond was certain her aunt had something particular to say. They sat close together. Still, the gathered trimming inside Rosamond’s bonnet was so delightful that Mrs. Bulstrode could not help wanting the same for Kate. Her rather fine eyes traveled around the whole generous circuit of it as she spoke.
“Rosamond, I’ve just heard something about you that surprised me very much.”
“What was it, Aunt?” Rosamond’s eyes were wandering too, over the broad embroidered collar her aunt wore.
“I can scarcely believe you would be engaged without my knowing—without your father telling me.” At last Mrs. Bulstrode’s eyes met her niece’s. Rosamond colored deeply before answering.
“But I’m not engaged, Aunt.”
“Then why does everyone say you are? Why is the whole town talking about it?”
“I don’t consider the town’s gossip very important,” Rosamond said, secretly pleased.

“Oh, darling, think more carefully. Don’t look down on your neighbors. Remember, you’re twenty-two now, and you won’t have a fortune. I’m certain your father won’t be able to set anything aside for you. Mr. Lydgate is intelligent and highly educated; I understand the attraction. I enjoy talking to men like that myself, and your uncle finds him very useful. But medicine pays poorly here. Of course this life isn’t everything, yet doctors seldom hold sound religious views. They’re too proud of their intellect. And you aren’t suited to marrying a poor man.
“Mr. Lydgate isn’t poor, Aunt. He has very distinguished relations.”
“He told me himself that he has little money.”
“Only because he’s accustomed to people who live in great style.”
“My dear Rosamond, you mustn’t expect to live in great style.”
Rosamond lowered her eyes and toyed with her bag. She was not hot-tempered and had no cutting replies to make, but she intended to live as she chose.

“Then it really is true?” Mrs. Bulstrode asked, studying her niece intently. “Your thoughts are fixed on Mr. Lydgate. There’s an understanding between you, even though your father hasn’t been told. Be honest with me, my dear. Has he actually proposed?”

Poor Rosamond was deeply uncomfortable. Until now she had been quite certain of Lydgate’s feelings and intentions. Faced with her aunt’s direct question, she hated being unable to answer yes. Her pride smarted, though her practiced control of her manner came to her aid.
“Please forgive me, Aunt. I’d prefer not to discuss it.”

“I hope you wouldn’t lose your heart without a definite prospect of marriage, darling. Think of the two excellent offers I know you’ve refused. One is still available, if you don’t throw the chance away. I knew a great beauty who ended up marrying badly through just that sort of behavior. Mr. Ned Plymdale is a pleasant young man; some would call him handsome. An only son, too. A substantial business like his is better than a profession. Marriage isn’t everything, of course. I would have you seek God’s kingdom first. But a girl ought to remain mistress of her own heart.”

“Even if I had it to give, I’d never give it to Mr. Ned Plymdale. I’ve already rejected him. If I loved someone, I would love immediately and forever,” Rosamond said, feeling very much the heroine of a romance and performing the role charmingly.
“I understand, my dear,” Mrs. Bulstrode said sadly as she stood to leave. “You’ve let yourself fall in love with someone who doesn’t return it.”
“No, Aunt, certainly not,” Rosamond answered with force.
“Then you’re completely sure Mr. Lydgate has serious feelings for you?”
Rosamond’s cheeks were now burning steadily, and she felt deeply humiliated. She remained silent. Her aunt left more convinced than ever.

In ordinary worldly matters Mr. Bulstrode generally followed his wife’s wishes. Without explaining why, she now asked him to discover, the next time he spoke to Lydgate, whether the doctor planned to marry soon. The answer was a definite no. Questioned further, Mr. Bulstrode made clear that Lydgate had spoken in a way no man could if he had an attachment likely to lead to marriage. Mrs. Bulstrode felt a serious duty had fallen to her. Before long she arranged a private conversation with Lydgate, moving from questions about Fred Vincy’s recovery and sincere expressions of concern for her brother’s large family to general observations on the difficulties young people faced in settling their futures. Young men often ran wild and disappointed their parents, giving little return for the money spent on them. Girls were exposed to many things that could damage their chances.

“Especially an attractive girl whose parents entertain a great deal,” Mrs. Bulstrode said. “Gentlemen monopolize her attention for the pleasure of the moment and drive other men away. To interfere with any girl’s prospects is a serious responsibility, Mr. Lydgate.” She fixed her gaze on him in unmistakable warning, if not reproach.

“Certainly,” Lydgate replied, looking back at her, perhaps even staring a little. “On the other hand, a man would have to be extraordinarily vain to think he must never pay attention to a young woman in case she falls in love with him—or other people assume she will.”

“Oh, Mr. Lydgate, you’re perfectly aware of your advantages. You know our young men here can’t compete with you. If you visit a house often, it may militate strongly against a girl’s making a suitable marriage. She may refuse other offers, if she receives any at all.”

Lydgate felt less flattered by his superiority to Middlemarch’s romantic heroes than irritated by his clear understanding of Mrs. Bulstrode’s purpose. She considered her words sufficiently impressive. By choosing the elevated word “militate,” she felt she had draped a dignified covering over a collection of particulars that nevertheless remained visible enough.

He was rather angry. One hand pushed back his hair; the other searched oddly in his waistcoat pocket. Then he bent to beckon the tiny black spaniel, which wisely declined his insincere offer of affection. He could not decently leave: he had dined there with other guests and had only just taken tea. Mrs. Bulstrode, however, was satisfied that he had understood her and changed the subject.

I believe Solomon’s Proverbs neglected to mention that just as a sore mouth discovers grit, an uneasy conscience detects hints. The next day, when Mr. Farebrother parted from Lydgate in the street, he remarked that they would probably meet at the Vincys’ that evening. Lydgate answered shortly that he had work to do and must give up going out at night.
“What, having yourself tied to the mast and plugging your ears?” the Vicar asked. “Well, if you don’t intend the sirens to win, you’re wise to take precautions early.”

A few days earlier Lydgate would have heard only the Vicar’s customary way of speaking. Now the words seemed loaded with a hint, confirming his impression that he had made a fool of himself and behaved in a way people could misread. Not Rosamond herself, he believed: surely she took it all as lightly as he meant it. Her tact and perception in matters of manners were exquisite. The people around her were the bunglers and busybodies. In any case, he would let the misunderstanding go no further. He resolved to visit Mr. Vincy’s only on business, and kept that resolution.

Rosamond grew very unhappy. The doubts her aunt had first raised increased day by day. After ten days without seeing Lydgate, they had become terror at the possible emptiness ahead, dread of the fatal sponge so readily and cheaply used to wipe away human hopes. The world would acquire a new desolation, like a wilderness briefly transformed by a magician into a garden. She felt she was learning the pain of disappointed love. No other man, she knew, could inspire the delightful castles in the air she had been building for six months. Poor Rosamond lost her appetite and felt as abandoned as Ariadne—a charming theatrical Ariadne stranded with all her trunks of costumes and no carriage in prospect.

Many astonishing mixtures go by the name of love, each claiming the rights of that sublime frenzy which, in books and plays, excuses everything. Fortunately Rosamond contemplated no desperate action. She braided her fair hair as beautifully as ever and maintained a proud composure. Her most comforting explanation was that Aunt Bulstrode had somehow intervened to stop Lydgate’s visits. Anything was preferable to indifference originating in himself. Anyone who thinks ten days too short—not to grow thin, lose weight, or show other measurable effects of passion, but to travel the entire inward circuit of anxious speculation and disappointment—knows little of what can happen in the elegant leisure of a young lady’s mind.

On the eleventh day, however, Mrs. Vincy stopped Lydgate as he was leaving Stone Court. Mr. Featherstone’s condition had changed significantly, and she wanted her husband to come that day. Would Lydgate pass on the message? He could have called at the warehouse. He could have torn a page from his notebook, written a message, and left it at the door. These simple alternatives apparently never occurred to him. We may infer that he had no great objection to visiting the house at an hour when Mr. Vincy would be out and leaving the message with Miss Vincy. A man may withhold his company for many reasons, but even a sage might dislike discovering that nobody missed him. A few playful remarks to Rosamond about resisting social distractions and resolving to go for long periods even without sweet music would make a graceful, easy connection between his old habits and the new. We must also admit that fleeting guesses about every possible reason for Mrs. Bulstrode’s hints had woven themselves, like fine clinging hairs, into the stronger fabric of his thoughts.

Miss Vincy was alone. When he entered, she blushed so intensely that he became embarrassed in turn. Instead of joking, he explained his errand at once and asked her, almost formally, to give her father the message. At first Rosamond had felt her happiness returning. His manner hurt her sharply. The blush disappeared, and she agreed coldly without a single unnecessary word. Some small piece of chainwork in her hands allowed her to avoid looking higher than his chin. In any failure, the beginning is certainly half the whole. After two long moments sitting there, shifting his whip and unable to speak, Lydgate stood to leave. Rosamond’s struggle between humiliation and the desire to hide it had made her nervous. She dropped the chain as though startled and rose automatically too. Lydgate instantly bent to retrieve it. When he straightened, he was very close to the lovely little face on its long fair neck, a face he was used to seeing turn with perfectly controlled, self-satisfied grace. This time, as he lifted his eyes, he saw a helpless trembling that moved him in an entirely new way and made him look sharply at her in question. At that moment she was as unguarded as she had ever been at five years old. She felt tears welling up. There was nothing to do but let them rest like water on a blue flower or spill down her cheeks, as they chose.

That instant of natural feeling was the feather-light touch that brings crystallization: it changed flirtation into love. Remember that the ambitious man looking at those blue forget-me-nots beneath the water was warm-hearted and impulsive. He had no idea what became of the chain. A thought had thrilled through his hidden depths and miraculously awakened the power of passionate love buried there—not in a sealed tomb, but under the thinnest, most easily broken earth. His words came abruptly and awkwardly, yet his voice turned them into an urgent declaration and appeal.
“What’s happened? You’re upset. Please tell me.”

Nobody had ever spoken to Rosamond in that voice. I am not sure she even knew what he had said. She only looked at him, and the tears ran down her face. No answer could have been more complete than that silence. Forgetting everything else, overwhelmed by tenderness at the sudden belief that this sweet young woman depended on him for happiness, Lydgate put his arms around her. He held her gently and protectively—gentleness toward the weak and suffering was familiar to him—and kissed away each of the two large tears. It was an unusual route to an understanding, but a short one. Rosamond was not offended. She drew back a little in shy happiness, and he could now sit beside her and speak more fully. She made her little confession; he poured out gratitude and tenderness with impulsive generosity. Half an hour later he left as an engaged man. His soul belonged no longer to himself, but to the woman to whom he had pledged it.

He returned that evening to speak to Mr. Vincy, who had just come home from Stone Court feeling certain he would soon hear of Mr. Featherstone’s demise. The fortunate word “demise” had come to him at exactly the right time and lifted his spirits above even their usual evening level. The right word always has power, lending its precision to what we do. Viewed as a demise, old Featherstone’s death became a purely legal event. Mr. Vincy could tap his snuffbox and be merry over it without even occasional pretensions to gravity. He hated both solemnity and pretense. Who ever stood in awe before a maker of wills, or sang a hymn over a title to land? That evening he was disposed to see everything cheerfully. He even told Lydgate that Fred had inherited the family constitution after all and would soon be as fine a young man as ever. Asked to approve Rosamond’s engagement, he agreed with astonishing ease, moving straight into general observations about the benefits of marriage for young men and women. From the whole discussion he apparently concluded that a little more punch would be appropriate.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXXII
paragraphs:
They’ll lap up the suggestion like cats drinking milk.
—SHAKESPEARE: The Tempest.

The Mayor’s triumphant confidence, based on Mr. Featherstone’s insistence that Fred and his mother stay with him, was a faint emotion beside the feelings stirring the old man’s blood relations. Now that he was confined to bed, they naturally displayed their family affection more openly and appeared in greater numbers. Naturally: when “poor Peter” had still occupied his chair in the paneled parlor, his impoverished relatives had been about as welcome at his hearth as the persistent beetles for which a cook prepares boiling water. Their Featherstone blood had been poorly fed through lack of money, not unwillingness to spend it. His brother Solomon and sister Jane, however, were rich. They did not consider the family frankness and complete absence of false courtesy with which Peter received them any reason to suppose that, when making his will, he would overlook the superior claims of wealth. He had at least never behaved so unnaturally as to banish them. It hardly seemed eccentric to keep away Jonah, Martha, and the rest, who could offer no comparable claims. They knew Peter’s maxim: money was a good egg and ought to be laid in a warm nest.

Jonah, Martha, and the other needy exiles saw matters differently. Probabilities vary as widely as the faces we can discover in carved patterns or wallpaper.
