Every shape is there, from Jupiter to Judy, if the imagination chooses to find it. The poorer, less favored relations thought Peter would probably remember them at the end precisely because he had done nothing for them while alive. Jonah argued that men liked their wills to surprise people. Martha said nobody ought to be surprised if he left most of his money to those least expecting it. Besides, surely a brother lying there with his legs swollen by dropsy must begin to feel that blood was thicker than water. Even if he did not change his will, he might have cash by him. At all events, some genuine relations ought to be on the premises, watching those who scarcely counted as relatives at all. Wills had been forged and contested before; such proceedings seemed to hold the golden, misty advantage of somehow supporting people who had been left nothing. And unrelated people might be caught carrying things off, with poor Peter helpless in bed! Someone ought to keep watch. On that point Solomon and Jane agreed with them. Various nephews, nieces, and cousins, reasoning still more subtly about the possible whims of a man free to will his property away however he pleased, felt generously that the family interest needed defending. Visiting Stone Court would only be right. Martha, now Mrs. Cranch, lived in the Chalky Flats and suffered from wheezing, so she could not make the journey. But her son, poor Peter’s own nephew, could represent her to advantage and keep Uncle Jonah from taking an unfair share of whatever unlikely events might occur. In short, the Featherstone blood carried a general conviction that everyone must watch everyone else, and that everyone else would do well to remember the Almighty was watching too.

Relations were therefore constantly arriving at Stone Court or leaving it. Mary Garth had the unpleasant job of taking their messages upstairs to Mr. Featherstone, who refused to see any of them, and the still more unpleasant job of returning with that answer. As housekeeper, she felt obliged by local hospitality to invite them to stay for a meal. But with Mr. Featherstone bedridden, she decided to consult Mrs. Vincy about the additional food being consumed downstairs.

“Oh, darling, when there’s property and someone’s dying, you must be generous. Heaven knows I don’t begrudge them every ham in the house—just keep the best for the funeral. Always have some stuffed veal ready, and a good cheese cut open. You have to expect an open house at a time like this,” said the hospitable Mrs. Vincy, whose cheerful voice and bright plumage had returned.

Some callers, however, arrived and stayed even after generous helpings of veal and ham. Brother Jonah was one. Most families contain such disagreeable members; perhaps the highest aristocracy has gigantic versions, with colossal debts and bloating purchased at greater expense. Jonah had come down in the world and chiefly supported himself by an occupation he modestly avoided boasting of, though it was much better than swindling on the stock exchange or the racecourse. It did not require him to remain in Brassing as long as he had a comfortable corner and plenty to eat elsewhere. He chose the kitchen corner, partly from preference and partly to avoid Solomon, of whom he held a strongly brotherly opinion. Sitting in an excellent armchair in his best suit, with good food always in sight, he enjoyed the comforting certainty of being on the premises, mingled with passing associations of Sunday and the bar at the Green Man. He informed Mary that he would remain within reach of Peter as long as the poor fellow was above ground. A family’s troublesome members are generally either its wits or its fools. Jonah was the Featherstones’ wit. He joked with the maids when they approached the fire, but treated Miss Garth as a suspicious person and followed her with a cold stare.

One pair of eyes would have been fairly easy for Mary to endure. Unfortunately, young Cranch had traveled all the way from the Chalky Flats to represent his mother and keep watch on Uncle Jonah. He too felt duty-bound to remain, chiefly in the kitchen, keeping his uncle company. Young Cranch did not stand exactly midway between wit and fool: he leaned a little toward the latter. His squint left his feelings uncertain, except that they were plainly not forceful. When Mary entered and Jonah’s cold, investigating eyes followed her, young Cranch turned the same way and seemed determined that she should notice his squint. It was as if he were doing it deliberately, like the gypsies when Borrow read the New Testament to them. This was a little too much for poor Mary. Sometimes it made her feel sick; sometimes she could hardly keep a straight face. Finding an opportunity one day, she could not resist describing the kitchen scene to Fred. Nothing would stop him going straight to see it, pretending merely to pass through. But the moment those four eyes faced him, he had to rush out through the nearest door, which led to the dairy. There, beneath the high roof among the milk pans, he gave way to laughter that echoed hollowly and could be heard perfectly in the kitchen. He escaped through another door. Jonah, who had not previously seen Fred’s pale complexion, long legs, and delicate, drawn face, prepared a store of sarcasms ingeniously combining these features with the lowest moral failings.

“Well, Tom, your trousers aren’t nearly so gentlemanly, are they? And your legs aren’t half so fine and long,” Jonah told his nephew, winking to suggest that these undeniable observations contained a deeper meaning. Tom looked down at his legs, without making clear whether he preferred his moral superiority to a more sinful length of limb and a disreputably refined pair of trousers.

There were watchful eyes in the large paneled parlor too, and close relatives eager to sit up through the night. Many people came, ate lunch, and went away. But Solomon and the lady who had been Jane Featherstone for twenty-five years before becoming Mrs. Waule found it worthwhile to stay for hours every day. Their only identifiable occupation was observing the crafty Mary Garth—so cunning that nothing could be detected against her—and producing occasional dry, wrinkled signs of tears over their exclusion from their brother’s room. These hinted at torrents possible in a wetter season. As the old man lost the strength to amuse himself with cutting remarks to his family, his dislike of them seemed to increase. Too weak to sting, he had all the more poison flowing back through his veins.

Distrusting Mary’s message, they had presented themselves together in the bedroom doorway. Both wore black. Mrs. Waule held a partly unfolded white handkerchief, and both faces were a sort of half-mourning purple. Meanwhile Mrs. Vincy, her cheeks pink and her pink ribbons fluttering, was actually giving their own brother a cordial. Pale Fred, with short curls such as one would naturally expect on a gambler, lounged comfortably in a large chair.

As soon as Featherstone saw these funeral figures appearing against his orders, anger strengthened him more effectively than the cordial. He lay supported by a bedrest, his gold-headed walking stick always beside him. Seizing it, he swept it back and forth as widely as his strength allowed, as though driving off hideous apparitions, and cried out in a hoarse shriek:
“Stay back, Mrs. Waule! Back, Solomon!”

“Oh, Brother Peter,” Mrs. Waule began, but Solomon raised a restraining hand. Nearly seventy, with broad cheeks and small, evasive eyes, he was far smoother-tempered than Peter and considered himself considerably shrewder. He was indeed unlikely to be deceived by anyone, since people could hardly be greedier or more dishonest than he already suspected. Even the unseen powers, he thought, might be soothed by an occasional gentle acknowledgment from a man of property who could have been as irreligious as other men.
“Brother Peter,” he said in a coaxing but solemnly official voice, “it’s only right that I speak to you about the Three Crofts and the Manganese. The Almighty knows what’s weighing on my mind—”

“Then he knows more than I care to,” Peter answered. He lowered his stick in a gesture of truce that also carried a threat: he turned it around so the gold head could serve as a club at close quarters, and stared at Solomon’s bald scalp.

“You may regret some things if you don’t talk to me, Brother,” Solomon said, though he came no nearer. “I’d gladly sit up with you tonight, and Jane too. You could speak whenever you felt ready, or let me speak.”
“Yes, I’ll choose my own time. You needn’t offer me yours,” Peter replied.

“You can’t choose your time to die, though, Brother,” Mrs. Waule began in her usual muffled voice. “And when you can’t speak, you may grow tired of strangers around you. You may think of me and my children.” Her voice broke at the touching thought she was assigning to her speechless brother. References to ourselves naturally move us.
“No, I won’t,” the old man contradicted her. “I won’t think of any of you. I’ve made my will, I tell you. It’s made.” He turned toward Mrs. Vincy and swallowed more cordial.
“Some people would be ashamed to take a place that rightfully belongs to others,” Mrs. Waule said, directing her narrow eyes the same way.
“Ah, Sister,” Solomon replied with soft irony, “you and I aren’t fashionable, handsome, or clever enough. We must be humble and let the smart people push ahead of us.”
Fred could not endure that. Standing and looking at Featherstone, he asked, “Would you like Mother and me to go, sir, so you can be alone with your friends?”

“Sit down, I tell you,” Featherstone snapped. “Stay where you are. Goodbye, Solomon.” He tried to brandish his stick again, but with the handle reversed he could no longer manage it. “Goodbye, Mrs. Waule. Don’t come back.”
“I’ll be downstairs, Brother, whatever you say,” Solomon answered. “I’ll do my duty. We’ll see what the Almighty permits.”

“Yes, where property passing out of families is concerned,” Mrs. Waule added. “Especially with steady young men ready to carry on. I pity the ones who aren’t steady, and I pity their mothers. Goodbye, Brother Peter.”

“Remember, I’m next eldest after you, Brother. I prospered from the start just as you did, and there’s land in the Featherstone name already through me,” Solomon said. He placed considerable faith in this reflection, which might recur to Peter during the night. “For the present, then, goodbye.”
They hurried their departure when they saw Featherstone tug both sides of his wig, shut his eyes, and stretch his mouth in a grimace, as though determined to become both deaf and blind.

Nevertheless, they came daily and sat downstairs at their post of duty. Sometimes they exchanged low remarks so slowly that an observer might have imagined two speaking machines, with the mechanism’s success still in doubt: would it function, or spend a long time winding itself up only to stick and remain silent? Solomon and Jane would have regretted being quick. Brother Jonah, on the other side of the wall, showed what that led to.

Visitors from nearby and farther away sometimes varied their watch in the paneled parlor. With Peter upstairs, his property could be discussed in the light of all the local knowledge available on the spot. Several country and Middlemarch neighbors agreed strongly with the family and supported their claims against the Vincys. Some women even wept while talking to Mrs. Waule, recalling their own past disappointments through additions to wills or spiteful marriages made by ungrateful elderly gentlemen who might have been expected to survive for a better purpose. Such conversations stopped abruptly when Mary entered, like an organ whose bellows suddenly fall idle. Every eye turned toward her as a possible beneficiary, or someone who might gain access to locked iron chests.

The younger men among the relations and family connections, however, found this uncertainty attractive. They saw a capable girl who, among all the possibilities in the air, might prove at least a modest prize. Mary therefore received her share of compliments and courteous attentions.

Chief among those paying them was Mr. Borthrop Trumbull, a distinguished local bachelor and auctioneer who handled many sales of land and cattle. He was a public figure, his name appearing on widely distributed posters, and might reasonably feel sorry for anyone who had never heard of him. A second cousin of Peter Featherstone’s, he had been more agreeably treated than the other relations because he was useful in business. The old man had named him a pallbearer in the funeral arrangements he had dictated himself. There was no ugly greed in Mr. Trumbull, only an honest appreciation of his own merits, which he knew might count against rivals if there were competition. If Peter Featherstone, who had behaved toward him as well as any living soul could, should have made him a handsome bequest, he could only say he had never angled for favor or flattered. He had merely given advice drawn from his experience: twenty years of it, beginning with his apprenticeship at fifteen, and likely to have produced knowledge of no underhand sort. His admiration was not confined to himself. Both privately and professionally, he enjoyed placing high values on things. He delighted in elevated phrases and never used an inferior expression without immediately correcting it. This was fortunate, since he spoke loudly and tended to dominate a room. He frequently stood or walked about, tugging down his waistcoat with the air of a man who strongly agreed with himself, rapidly straightening his appearance with a forefinger, and marking each fresh sequence of movements by busily handling his large watch seals. A certain fierceness sometimes entered his manner, but it was mostly directed at mistaken opinions. There are so many of those to correct that a man with reading and experience must naturally have his patience tried. He considered the Featherstones generally limited in understanding, but as a worldly man and public figure he took them as he found them. He even went to converse with Jonah and young Cranch in the kitchen, certain that his searching questions about the Chalky Flats had greatly impressed the latter. If anyone had remarked that an auctioneer had to understand the nature of everything, Mr. Trumbull would have smiled and silently adjusted his appearance, feeling that he came close to it. On the whole, in the auctioneering line, he was honorable and unashamed of his business. He believed that “the celebrated Peel, now Sir Robert,” if introduced to him, would certainly recognize his importance.

“I wouldn’t object to a slice of that ham and a glass of that ale, Miss Garth, if you’ll permit me,” he said, entering the parlor at half past eleven. He had enjoyed the rare privilege of seeing Featherstone and now stood with his back to the fire between Solomon and Mrs. Waule.
“No need for you to leave the room. Allow me to ring.”
“Thank you, but I have something to do,” Mary answered.
“Well, Mr. Trumbull, you’re certainly a favorite,” Mrs. Waule observed.
“What, because I’ve seen the old gentleman?” The auctioneer handled his seals impartially. “Yes, well, he’s relied on me a good deal.” He pressed his lips together and frowned thoughtfully.
“May a man ask what his own brother has been saying?” Solomon inquired in a softly humble voice. Being rich and under no necessity to humble himself, he enjoyed the luxurious cunning of it.

“Certainly anyone may ask,” Mr. Trumbull replied with loud, good-natured but cutting sarcasm. “Anyone may interrogate. Anyone may give his observations an interrogative form.” His voice grew more resonant as his language rose. “Good speakers do it constantly, even when they expect no reply. We call it a figure of speech—speech at a high figure, one might say.” The eloquent auctioneer smiled at his own cleverness.
“I wouldn’t be sorry to hear he’d remembered you, Mr. Trumbull,” Solomon said. “I’ve never objected to deserving people. It’s the undeserving I object to.”

“Ah, that’s the point, you see. Precisely the point,” Mr. Trumbull said meaningfully. “There’s no denying that undeserving people have received legacies—even the residue of estates. Such things happen with testamentary dispositions.” Again he pursed his lips and frowned a little.
“Are you saying you know my brother has left his land outside the family, Mr. Trumbull?” Mrs. Waule asked. Not naturally hopeful, she found those long words depressing.
“He might as well hand the land straight to a charity as leave it to certain people,” Solomon remarked when his sister’s question received no answer.
“What, to a Blue-Coat charity school?” Mrs. Waule asked again. “Oh, Mr. Trumbull, surely you don’t mean that! It would defy the Almighty who made him prosper.”

While she spoke, Trumbull strolled from the hearth toward the window. His forefinger patrolled the inside of his neckcloth, then his whiskers and the curves of his hair. He moved to Miss Garth’s worktable, opened a book lying there, and read the title with the pompous emphasis of an auction announcement.

“‘Anne of Geierstein’”—he pronounced it “Jeersteen”—“‘or the Maiden of the Mist, by the author of Waverley.’” Turning the page, he began in a sonorous voice: “Almost four centuries have passed since the events described in the following chapters occurred on the Continent.” He placed the stress on the last syllable of that excellent final word. It was not ignorance of ordinary usage: he felt his novel pronunciation enhanced the rich sound he had given the whole passage.

Just then the servant arrived with the tray, safely carrying the moment for answering Mrs. Waule past. She and Solomon had watched his movements with the feeling that advanced learning sadly obstructed serious business. In truth, Mr. Trumbull knew nothing about the will. Short of being arrested for concealing treason, however, he could hardly have been made to admit ignorance of anything.

“Only a mouthful of ham and a glass of ale,” he said reassuringly. “A man with public duties must eat when he can. I’d back this ham against any in the three kingdoms,” he added after swallowing several bites at alarming speed. “Better than the hams at Freshitt Hall, in my judgment—and I consider myself a reasonably good judge.”
“Some people don’t care for so much sugar in a ham,” Mrs. Waule said. “My poor brother always insisted on it.”

“If anyone wants something better, they’re welcome to ask. But bless my soul, what a fragrance! I’d be glad to buy that quality. A gentleman feels a certain satisfaction”—his voice took on an emotional protest—“when a ham like this appears on his table.”

He pushed away his plate, poured himself ale, and drew his chair forward a little. The movement gave him a chance to inspect the insides of his legs, which he stroked approvingly. Mr. Trumbull possessed all those less frivolous gestures and mannerisms that distinguish the dominant peoples of the north.

“I see you have an interesting volume, Miss Garth,” he remarked when Mary returned. “By the author of ‘Waverley,’ which means Sir Walter Scott. I’ve bought one of his books myself: a very fine thing, an extremely superior publication, called ‘Ivanhoe.’ You won’t soon find a writer to beat him, I think—or, in my opinion, he will not speedily be surpassed. I’ve just read a passage at the commencement of ‘Anne of Jeersteen.’ It commences well.” Nothing ever began for Mr. Trumbull: in conversation as on his sale notices, it always commenced. “You’re fond of reading, evidently. Do you subscribe to the Middlemarch library?”
“No,” Mary replied. “Mr. Fred Vincy brought me this.”

“I’m quite a bookman myself,” Trumbull continued. “No fewer than two hundred volumes bound in calfskin, and well chosen, I flatter myself. Pictures too, by Murillo, Rubens, Teniers, Titian, Vandyck, and others. I’d gladly lend you any volume you cared to name, Miss Garth.”
“Thank you very much,” said Mary, hurrying off again, “but I have little time to read.”
“I’d say my brother has provided for her in his will,” Solomon murmured once the door closed, nodding toward the absent Mary.
“His first wife wasn’t much of a match for him,” Mrs. Waule said. “She brought no money. And this girl is only her niece—and a very proud girl too. My brother has always paid her wages.”

“A sensible young woman, in my opinion,” said Trumbull, draining his ale and rising with a forceful adjustment of his waistcoat. “I’ve watched her measure medicine by the drop. She pays attention to her task, sir. A great advantage in a woman, and for our friend upstairs, poor dear old soul. A man whose life has value ought to consider his wife as a nurse. That’s what I’d do if I married, and I believe I’ve been single long enough to avoid mistakes in that direction. Some men need marriage to raise them a little. If I ever need that, I hope someone will tell me—I hope some individual will inform me of the fact. Good morning, Mrs. Waule. Good morning, Mr. Solomon. I trust our next meeting will take place under less sorrowful circumstances.”
After Trumbull left with an impressive bow, Solomon leaned toward his sister. “Depend on it, Jane, my brother has left that girl a great lump of money.”
“You’d certainly think so from Mr. Trumbull’s manner,” Jane replied. After a pause she added, “He talks as though my daughters couldn’t be trusted to measure drops.”
“Auctioneers talk extravagantly,” Solomon said. “Though Trumbull has certainly made money.”

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXXIII
paragraphs: Shortly after midnight Mary Garth took over the watch in Mr. Featherstone’s room and remained alone with him through the early hours. She often chose this duty and found some pleasure in it, despite his irritability whenever he needed her. Between his demands she could sit completely still, enjoying the surrounding quiet and the dim light. The red fire, with its soft sounds of movement, seemed a solemn form of life, serenely independent of the petty passions, foolish desires, and pursuit of worthless uncertainties that daily provoked her contempt. Mary enjoyed her own thoughts and could entertain herself well in the half-light with her hands in her lap. She had learned early, and for compelling reasons, that the world was unlikely to arrange itself for her particular satisfaction. She wasted no time being astonished or offended by the fact. Already she largely regarded life as a comedy in which she had proudly—even generously—resolved never to play the mean or treacherous part. She might have grown cynical without parents she respected and a deep reserve of loving gratitude, made fuller by her refusal to expect too much.

Tonight, as usual, she turned over the day’s scenes. Her lips often curled in amusement at oddities her imagination made funnier still. People and their illusions were so absurd: wearing fools’ caps without knowing it, imagining their own lies opaque while everyone else’s were transparent, exempting themselves from every rule, as though a lamp that made the whole world yellow left them alone rosy. Yet some illusions she witnessed did not seem entirely comic. With no evidence beyond her close study of Featherstone’s character, she privately believed the Vincys were as likely to be disappointed as the relations he kept away, however much he liked having them around. She felt considerable contempt for Mrs. Vincy’s obvious fear of leaving her alone with Fred. Even so, she worried about how Fred would bear it if his uncle left him as poor as before. In his presence she could make him the target of a joke; in his absence his foolishness gave her no pleasure.

Still, she enjoyed thinking. A vigorous young mind not overwhelmed by passion finds satisfaction in learning about life and takes an interested view of its own developing powers. Mary had plenty of laughter inside her.

No solemnity or sorrow for the old man in the bed ran through these reflections. Such emotions are easier to pretend than to feel toward someone whose remaining life seems to consist only of surviving vices. Mary had always known Featherstone at his least pleasant. He took no pride in her; she was merely useful. Concern for a soul that constantly snaps at you must be left to earthly saints, and Mary was no saint. She had never answered him harshly and had served him faithfully. That was as far as she could go. Featherstone himself felt no concern for his soul and had refused to discuss it with Mr. Tucker.

Tonight he had not snapped at her. For the first hour or two he lay unusually still. At last she heard his bunch of keys rattle against the tin box he always kept beside him in bed. Around three o’clock he said with striking clarity, “Come here, missy!”

Mary went to him. He had already pulled the box from under the bedclothes, though he generally asked her to do it, and had chosen the key. Unlocking it, he took out another key and looked directly at her. His eyes seemed to have regained all their sharpness. “How many of them are in the house?”
“You mean your own relations, sir?” Mary asked, familiar with his way of speaking. He gave a slight nod, and she continued.
“Mr. Jonah Featherstone and young Cranch are staying overnight.”
“Ah, so they’re sticking, are they? And the others come every day, I suppose—Solomon, Jane, all the youngsters? Peeping about, counting up, doing their sums?”
“They don’t all come daily. Mr. Solomon and Mrs. Waule do, and the others visit often.”

He listened with a grimace, then relaxed his face. “More fools them. Listen, missy. It’s three in the morning, and my mind’s as clear as it ever was. I know every bit of my property, where the money’s invested, everything. I’ve arranged it all so I can change my mind and please myself at the end. Do you hear? I have all my faculties.”
“Yes, sir?” Mary answered calmly.

He lowered his voice, looking more cunning still. “I’ve made two wills, and I mean to burn one. Do exactly what I say. This key opens the iron chest in that cupboard. Push hard beside the brass plate at the top until it slides like a bolt. Then put the key in the front lock and turn it. Go and do it. Take the top paper out. ‘Last Will and Testament,’ printed large.”
“No, sir,” Mary said firmly. “I can’t do that.”
“Can’t? I’m telling you that you must.” His voice began to tremble at the shock of resistance.
“I can’t touch your chest or your will. I have to refuse anything that could expose me to suspicion.”
“I tell you, I’m perfectly sane. Am I not to do what I choose at the end? I made two wills for this very reason. Take the key.”
“No, sir. I won’t,” Mary answered with greater firmness. Her aversion was growing.
“There’s no time to waste, I tell you.”
“I can’t help that, sir. I won’t let the end of your life stain the beginning of mine. I will not touch the chest or your will.” She stepped back from the bed.
He stared blankly for a while, holding the single key upright on its ring. Then, with an agitated jerk, he began using his bony left hand to empty the tin box in front of him.
“Missy,” he said hurriedly, “look! Take the money, the banknotes and the gold. Here, take it! You can have the lot. Just do as I say.”
He strained to reach the key toward her. Mary stepped farther away.
“I won’t touch either the key or the money, sir. Please don’t ask again. If you do, I’ll have to fetch your brother.”

His hand fell. For the first time Mary saw Peter Featherstone cry like a child. “Please put your money away, sir,” she said as gently as she could. Then she returned to her chair beside the fire, hoping to show him that further demands would be useless. After a while he recovered himself and spoke eagerly.
“Then listen. Fetch the young fellow. Fetch Fred Vincy.”
Mary’s heart quickened. Possibilities rushed through her mind about what destroying a second will might mean. She had to make a difficult choice at once.
“I’ll fetch him if you let me bring Mr. Jonah and some others too.”
“No one else. Just the young fellow. I’ll do what I please.”
“Wait until daylight, sir, when everyone’s up. Or shall I call Simmons now and send him for the lawyer? He could be here within two hours.”
“The lawyer? What do I want him for? No one is to know. No one, I tell you. I’ll do as I please.”

“Please let me bring someone else, sir,” Mary urged. She felt uncomfortable alone with him. A strange flare of nervous energy seemed to let him speak repeatedly without breaking into his usual cough. Yet she did not want to upset him further by opposing him unnecessarily. “Please let me call somebody.”
“Leave me alone, I say. Look, missy, take the money. You’ll never get another chance. Nearly two hundred, and there’s more in the box. Nobody knows how much was here. Take it and do what I tell you.”

Standing by the fire, Mary watched its red light fall on the old man, propped against his pillows and bedrest, his skeletal hand extending the key and the money spread on the quilt. She never forgot that picture of a man determined to have his own way at the end. But the manner of his offer made her refusal harder and more resolute than ever.
“It’s useless, sir. I won’t do it. Put the money away. I won’t touch it. I’ll do anything else I can to make you comfortable, but I will not touch your keys or your money.”
“Anything else! Anything else!” he rasped furiously. As in a nightmare, he struggled to shout but could scarcely be heard. “I want nothing else. Come here. Come here!”

Knowing him too well, Mary approached cautiously. He dropped his keys and tried to seize the walking stick, staring at her like an old hyena. The effort in his hand twisted the muscles of his face. She stopped beyond his reach.
“Let me give you a little cordial,” she said quietly. “Try to calm yourself. Perhaps you’ll sleep. Tomorrow, when it’s light, you can do what you want.”

Although she was out of range, he lifted the stick and threw it with a violent effort that achieved nothing. It slipped over the foot of the bed and fell. Mary left it there and went back to the fireside. She would bring the cordial later; exhaustion would quiet him. The coldest hour of the morning was approaching. The fire had burned low, and through the gap in the heavy woolen curtains she could see the pale light filtered by the blind. She added wood to the fire, wrapped herself in a shawl, and sat down, hoping he would sleep now. Going near him might only prolong his irritation. He had said nothing since throwing the stick, though she had watched him pick up his keys again and rest his right hand on the money. He did not put it away, and she thought he was falling asleep.
Now, however, the memory of what had happened troubled Mary more than the event itself. She began to question decisions that had felt imperative at the critical moment and had left no room for doubt.

The dry wood suddenly flared, lighting every corner. She saw him lying still, his head turned slightly aside. She approached without a sound. His face seemed strangely motionless, but then the shifting firelight made everything appear to move, and she was unsure. Her heart beat so violently that she distrusted her senses. Even after touching him and listening for his breath, she could not trust her conclusion. She went to the window and gently held back the curtain and blind, letting the steady light of the sky fall across the bed.

A moment later she rushed to the bell and rang hard. Very soon there was no doubt: Peter Featherstone was dead, his right hand gripping the keys and his left resting on the pile of banknotes and gold.

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXIV
paragraphs:
“1_st Gent_. Such men as this are feathers, chips, and straws,
Carry no weight, no force.

2_d Gent_. But levity
Is causal too, and makes the sum of weight.
For power finds its place in lack of power;
Advance is cession, and the driven ship
May run aground because the helmsman’s thought
Lacked force to balance opposites.”

Peter Featherstone was buried one May morning. May in the unromantic neighborhood of Middlemarch did not always mean warmth and sunshine. That morning a cold wind swept blossoms out of the neighboring gardens and across the grassy mounds of Lowick churchyard. Racing clouds occasionally let through a shaft of light, gilding whatever happened to stand beneath it, beautiful or ugly alike. There was an unusually varied collection of objects in the churchyard, where a small crowd of country people had gathered to watch the funeral. Word had spread that it would be a “big burying.” The old gentleman had left detailed written instructions: he intended to outdo his social superiors in the splendor of his funeral. And so he had. Old Featherstone was no Harpagon, whose other passions had been swallowed by the eternally starved appetite for saving money, and who would have negotiated with his undertaker in advance. He loved money, but he also enjoyed spending it to satisfy his particular tastes. Perhaps what he enjoyed most was its power to make other people uncomfortably aware of his influence. Anyone who insists that old Featherstone must have had some good qualities will find no contradiction from me. Still, goodness is modest and easily discouraged. When shameless vices push it aside early in life, it tends to withdraw into such deep seclusion that people constructing a selfish old gentleman in theory find it easier to believe in than those whose more limited judgments come from knowing him. At any rate, he had set his heart on a grand funeral, attended by invited guests who would have preferred to stay home. He had even specified that his female relatives should follow him to the grave. Poor sister Martha had therefore made a troublesome journey from the Chalky Flats. She and Jane would have found tearful comfort in this proof that a brother who disliked their company while alive had looked forward to having it once he became a testator. Unfortunately the same invitation had gone to Mrs. Vincy, making its meaning doubtful. Her lavish expenditure on fine crape suggested the most presumptuous expectations. Worse still, her rosy complexion advertised that she was no blood relation, but belonged to that generally objectionable category, a wife's family.

Everyone has some imagination, since images are the offspring of desire. Poor old Featherstone, who often laughed at other people's self-deceptions, shared their illusions nevertheless. When he wrote the program for his burial, he certainly never made himself understand that he could enjoy his part in this little drama only in anticipation. As he chuckled over the troubles his dead hand would still have the grip to cause, he inevitably imagined his own awareness inhabiting that pale, motionless body. Whatever thought he gave to a future life was thus a thought of satisfaction enjoyed inside his coffin. Old Featherstone, too, was imaginative in his way.

The three mourning coaches were duly filled as the dead man's instructions required. Mounted pallbearers wore the finest scarves and hatbands, and even the men carrying the coffin had been furnished with substantial, expensive signs of grief. Once on foot, the black procession looked still larger in the little churchyard. The heavy faces and dark clothes trembling in the wind seemed to belong to a world strangely at odds with the drifting blossoms and the sunlight flashing on the daisies. Mr. Cadwallader met them as officiating clergyman, again at Peter Featherstone's express request, and again for characteristic reasons. He despised curates, invariably calling them understrappers, and had determined to be buried by a clergyman with a living of his own. Mr. Casaubon would never have done. Quite apart from his unwillingness to perform such duties, Featherstone particularly disliked him as his own rector, with a claim on his land through the tithe, and as the preacher of morning sermons through which the old man, wide awake in his pew, had been obliged to sit inwardly snarling. He objected to a parson perched above his head and preaching at him. With Mr. Cadwallader things had been different. The trout stream running through Mr. Casaubon's land also crossed Featherstone's, so this was a parson who had needed to ask a favor instead of delivering a sermon. Besides, he belonged to the upper gentry four miles from Lowick. Distance raised him into the same lofty sphere as the county sheriff and other dignitaries vaguely understood to be necessary to the order of things. Being buried by Mr. Cadwallader would be gratifying; even his name provided an excellent opportunity for deliberate mispronunciation.

It was this honor paid to the Rector of Tipton and Freshitt that brought Mrs. Cadwallader into the party watching old Featherstone's funeral from an upstairs window at the manor. She did not much enjoy visiting the house. But, as she put it, she liked inspecting collections of curious animals, and the funeral promised just such a collection. To make the visit thoroughly agreeable, she had persuaded Sir James and the young Lady Chettam to drive her and the Rector to Lowick.
“I'll go wherever you like with you, Mrs. Cadwallader,” Celia had said. “Only I don't like funerals.”

“My dear, with a clergyman in the family you have to adjust your tastes. I learned that very early. On marrying Humphrey, I resolved to enjoy sermons. I began by being extremely fond of the end. The feeling soon extended to the middle and beginning, since I couldn't have the end without them.”
“Certainly you couldn't,” the Dowager Lady Chettam agreed with dignified emphasis.

The window commanding the funeral belonged to the room Mr. Casaubon had used while forbidden to work. Despite warnings and prescriptions, however, he had now returned to almost all his old habits. After greeting Mrs. Cadwallader politely, he had slipped back into the library to ruminate over a learned misconception concerning Cush and Mizraim.

Without these visitors, Dorothea might also have remained shut in the library. She would then have missed old Featherstone's funeral, a scene apparently remote from the concerns of her own life, yet one which afterward returned whenever certain tender places in her memory were touched, just as her vision of St. Peter's in Rome had become woven into feelings of despondency. Events that transform our neighbors' lives form only the background to our own. Yet, like some particular appearance of fields and trees, they become linked with periods in our personal history. They enter the unity of experience created by the things we feel most intensely.

This dreamlike connection between something strange and poorly understood and the deepest secrets of her experience seemed to reflect Dorothea's loneliness—a loneliness arising from the very intensity of her nature. The country gentry of earlier times breathed a thin social atmosphere. Scattered on separate stations high up the mountain, they looked down without distinguishing much in the denser layers of life below. Dorothea felt uncomfortable with both the view and the chill of that elevation.

“I've seen enough,” Celia said when the procession had gone into the church. She moved just behind her husband's elbow, where she could secretly brush his coat with her cheek. “I expect Dodo enjoys it. She likes sad things and ugly people.”

“I like learning something about the people around me,” said Dorothea, who had watched everything with a monk's curiosity on a holiday excursion. “We seem to know nothing about our neighbors unless they live in cottages. I keep wondering how other people live, and how things affect them. I'm very grateful to Mrs. Cadwallader for coming and getting me out of the library.”

“And grateful you ought to be,” Mrs. Cadwallader replied. “Your prosperous Lowick farmers are as remarkable as buffaloes or bison. I doubt you see half of them in church. They are nothing like your uncle's tenants, or Sir James's. Monstrosities—farmers with no landlords! One hardly knows where to put them.”

“Most of the mourners aren't from Lowick,” Sir James said. “I imagine they're people expecting legacies, from farther away or from Middlemarch. Lovegood says the old man has left a considerable sum of money besides his land.”

“Just imagine! While so many younger sons can't afford their own dinners,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. The door opened and she turned. “Ah, Mr. Brooke! I felt there was someone missing, and now I know who. You've come to watch this extraordinary funeral, of course?”

“No, to inquire after Casaubon—see how he's getting along, you know. And to bring some news—a little news for you, my dear.” Mr. Brooke nodded at Dorothea as she approached him. “I peeped into the library and found Casaubon at his books. I told him it was no use. ‘This won't do at all,’ I said. ‘You must think of your wife, Casaubon.’ He promised to join us. I didn't give him my news. I told him he must come upstairs.”

“Look, they're leaving the church now!” cried Mrs. Cadwallader. “Good heavens, what a wonderfully assorted company! There's Mr. Lydgate, in his medical capacity, I suppose. But that woman is really handsome, and the fair-haired young man must be her son. Do you know who they are, Sir James?”
“I can see Vincy, the Middlemarch mayor. Presumably that's his wife and son,” Sir James answered. He looked to Mr. Brooke for confirmation; Mr. Brooke nodded and said—
“Yes, a thoroughly respectable family. Vincy is an excellent fellow, a credit to the manufacturers. You've met him at my house, you know.”
“Oh yes—one of your secret committee,” Mrs. Cadwallader said mischievously.
“He goes coursing, though,” said Sir James, with a fox-hunter's contempt.

“And helps drain the life out of those miserable handloom weavers at Tipton and Freshitt. That explains his family's smooth skins and healthy looks,” Mrs. Cadwallader said. “Those dark, purple-faced creatures set them off admirably. Goodness, they look like a row of jugs! Look at Humphrey. In his white surplice, towering over them, he might be an ugly archangel.”
“A funeral is a solemn business all the same,” Mr. Brooke observed, “when you look at it that way, you know.”
“But I don't look at it that way. If I wore my solemnity too frequently, it would fall to pieces. The old man's time had come, and nobody there regrets it.”
“How dreadful,” said Dorothea. “I think this funeral is the saddest sight I've ever seen. It darkens the whole morning. I can't bear the thought of anyone dying without leaving love behind.”

She meant to continue, but noticed her husband entering and taking a seat a little apart. His presence did not always change her feelings happily. She sensed that he often silently disapproved of what she said.

“Really!” Mrs. Cadwallader exclaimed. “A new face has appeared from behind that broad man, stranger than any of the others. A little round head with protruding eyes—quite froglike. Do look. Surely he belongs to a different family.”

“Let me look!” said Celia, newly curious. Standing behind Mrs. Cadwallader, she leaned forward over her head. “What a peculiar face!” Then a different surprise suddenly changed her expression. “Dodo! You never mentioned that Mr. Ladislaw had come back!”
Alarm struck Dorothea. Everyone saw her turn abruptly pale and look straight up at her uncle, while Mr. Casaubon watched her.

“He came along with me, you know. He's my guest—staying at the Grange,” said Mr. Brooke with perfect ease. He nodded at Dorothea as though this were precisely the news she should have expected. “We've brought the picture on top of the carriage too. I knew you'd enjoy the surprise, Casaubon. Your very likeness—as Aquinas, you know. Exactly the right thing. And you'll hear young Ladislaw explain it. He talks remarkably well—draws your attention to this and that—understands art and all those matters. Excellent company, you know. Whatever line you take, he can keep up with you. Just what I've wanted for ages.”

Mr. Casaubon gave a cold, courteous bow. He controlled his irritation only enough to remain silent. Will's letter was as present to his mind as to Dorothea's. He had noticed its absence from the letters set aside for him during his recovery. Privately deciding that Dorothea must have written to tell Will not to come to Lowick, he had been too proudly sensitive to bring the matter up again. Now he concluded that she had arranged for her uncle to invite Will to the Grange. Dorothea felt quite unable to explain anything at that moment.

Mrs. Cadwallader had turned her eyes from the churchyard and observed a good deal of silent communication. Finding it less clear than she would have liked, she could not help asking, “Who is this Mr. Ladislaw?”

“A young relation of Mr. Casaubon's,” Sir James answered at once. Kindness often made him perceptive and quick in personal affairs. From Dorothea's look toward her husband, he had guessed that something frightened her.

“A most agreeable young man. Casaubon has provided everything for him,” Mr. Brooke explained. “He's a good return on your expenditure, Casaubon,” he continued, nodding encouragingly. “I hope he'll stay a long time, and we'll get somewhere with my papers. I have any number of ideas and facts, you know. I can see he's exactly the fellow to arrange them. Remembers the appropriate quotations, _omne tulit punctum_, and so on—puts things in a particular light. I asked him some time back, Casaubon, while you were ill. Dorothea said you couldn't receive visitors, you know, and asked me to write.”

Poor Dorothea felt that each word her uncle uttered must irritate Mr. Casaubon like a grain of sand in his eye. To explain now that she had never wanted her uncle to invite Will Ladislaw would have been utterly inappropriate. She could not begin to understand her husband's reasons for disliking his presence, although the scene in the library had made that dislike painfully clear. But she knew it would be wrong to say anything that let other people suspect it. Mr. Casaubon himself had not fully examined his mixed motives. Like the rest of us, when irritated he looked for justification rather than self-understanding. He did, however, want to conceal his feelings. Only Dorothea could detect the changes in his face before he spoke, bowing more ceremoniously and making his voice rise and fall more than usual—
“Your hospitality is most generous, my dear sir. I must express my gratitude for your extending it to a member of my family.”
By now the funeral had finished, and people were leaving the churchyard.
“You can see him now, Mrs. Cadwallader,” Celia said. “He looks exactly like the miniature of Mr. Casaubon's aunt in Dorothea's boudoir. Quite good-looking.”
“A very pretty young shoot,” Mrs. Cadwallader remarked dryly. “What profession is your nephew to follow, Mr. Casaubon?”
“Excuse me: he is my cousin, not my nephew.”

“Well, he's trying out his wings, you know,” Mr. Brooke broke in. “Exactly the kind of young man who gets ahead. I'd be pleased to give him a chance. He could be a fine secretary, for instance—like Hobbes, or Milton, or Swift. That type of fellow.”
“I see,” said Mrs. Cadwallader. “Someone to write speeches.”

“Shall I bring him in now, Casaubon?” Mr. Brooke asked. “He wouldn't enter until I'd announced him, you know. Then we can go downstairs and inspect the picture. It's your exact likeness: a profound, subtle thinker, forefinger resting on the page, while Saint Bonaventure, or somebody, a rather stout, rosy fellow, gazes up at the Trinity. Everything has a symbolic meaning, you know. The higher kind of art. I like it within limits, but not beyond them. Keeping up with it becomes rather a strain. You're quite at home there, though, Casaubon. And your painter does flesh well—weight, transparency, all that. I studied those matters quite deeply once. Anyway, I'll fetch Ladislaw.”

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXV
paragraphs:
“Non, je ne comprends pas de plus charmant plaisir
Que de voir d’héritiers une troupe affligée
Le maintien interdit, et la mine allongée,
Lire un long testament où pales, étonnés
On leur laisse un bonsoir avec un pied de nez.
Pour voir au naturel leur tristesse profonde
Je reviendrais, je crois, exprès de l’autre monde.”
—REGNARD: _Le Légataire Universel_.

When the animals went into the Ark two by two, we may suppose that related species had plenty to say privately about one another. They must have been tempted to consider the existence of so many creatures, all eating from the same supply, distinctly unnecessary, since it reduced everyone's share. (I fear the vultures' part in the proceedings would be too distressing for art to portray. Their throats are unflatteringly bare, and they appear to have no rituals or ceremonies.)

A similar temptation beset the Christian flesh-eaters in Peter Featherstone's funeral procession. Most had their thoughts fixed on a finite supply from which each wanted the largest possible share. The established blood relations and relations by marriage already formed a sizable company. Multiply their number by all the possible outcomes, and there was ample scope for jealous speculation and touching hopes. Resentment of the Vincys had united everyone of Featherstone blood in a common hostility. Until some definite sign emerged that one of their own number would receive more than the others, their chief anxiety must be that long-legged Fred Vincy would get the land. This still left them plenty of feeling and leisure for less definite jealousies, including their jealousy of Mary Garth. Solomon found time to consider how little Jonah deserved, and Jonah to call Solomon greedy. Jane, the elder sister, thought Martha's children had no right to expect as much as the young Waules. Martha, less committed to the rights of the firstborn, regretted Jane's acquisitiveness. These immediate relations naturally felt how unreasonable it was for cousins and second cousins to entertain hopes at all. They calculated how alarmingly small legacies could add up if there were too many. Two cousins had come to hear the will, and one second cousin besides Mr. Trumbull. This other second cousin was a Middlemarch dealer in fabrics, a polite man who added h's where they did not belong. Both cousins were elderly men from Brassing. One based his claim on the inconvenient expense he had incurred sending oysters and other delicacies to his wealthy cousin Peter. The other, a thoroughly gloomy man resting his hands and chin on a stick, felt entitled on the grounds of general merit, rather than any narrowly defined service. Both were irreproachable citizens of Brassing who wished Jonah Featherstone did not live there. A family's wit is generally appreciated most by outsiders.

“Trumbull alone is pretty certain of five hundred—you can count on _that_. I wouldn't be surprised if my brother promised it,” Solomon had reflected aloud to his sisters on the evening before the funeral.
“Dear me, dear me!” said poor sister Martha. Her habitual notion of hundreds had scarcely extended beyond the amount of rent she owed.

By morning, however, the appearance of an unknown mourner had upset every familiar line of speculation. He seemed to have splashed down among them from the moon. This was the man Mrs. Cadwallader called frog-faced: perhaps thirty-two or thirty-three, with protruding eyes, a thin-lipped mouth curved downward, and hair brushed smoothly back from a forehead which receded abruptly above the brows. His face certainly had a frog's fixed expression. Here, plainly, was another beneficiary; why else invite him to mourn? New possibilities brought fresh uncertainty and almost silenced conversation in the mourning coaches. We all feel humbled by the sudden discovery of a fact that has existed quite comfortably, perhaps privately staring at us, while we have been constructing a world that leaves it out altogether. Nobody had previously seen this dubious stranger except Mary Garth. All she knew was that twice, when Mr. Featherstone was still coming downstairs, he had visited Stone Court and remained alone with him for several hours. She had managed to tell her father. Perhaps Caleb's eyes, apart from the lawyer's, were the only ones studying the stranger with curiosity rather than disgust or suspicion. Expecting little and coveting still less, Caleb Garth wanted to see whether his guesses would prove right. As the unknown mourner, whose name they gathered was Rigg, entered the paneled parlor and sat near the door to hear the will, Caleb rubbed his chin with a half-smile and cast intelligent glances at him much as he might appraise a tree. His composure contrasted strikingly with the alarm or contempt on other faces. Solomon and Jonah had just gone upstairs with the lawyer to find the will. Noticing two empty chairs between herself and Mr. Borthrop Trumbull, Mrs. Waule summoned the courage to move beside that great authority. He was fingering his watch seals and arranging his appearance, determined to betray neither wonder nor surprise—both so compromising to a man of ability.
“I expect you know all about what my poor brother's arranged, Mr. Trumbull,” Mrs. Waule said in her softest muffled voice, turning her crape-shaded bonnet toward his ear.
“My dear lady, anything communicated to me was communicated in confidence,” the auctioneer answered, raising a hand as if to shield the secret.
“People who've counted on their good fortune may find themselves mistaken yet,” Mrs. Waule went on, somewhat relieved by saying so.
“Expectations frequently mislead us,” said Mr. Trumbull, maintaining their confidential tone.
“Ah!” Mrs. Waule looked across at the Vincys, then returned to the chair beside her sister Martha.

“Poor Peter was amazingly secretive,” she said, still in an undertone. “Not one of us knows what he may have had on his conscience. I only hope, Martha, his way of life wasn't worse than we've supposed.”

Poor Mrs. Cranch was stout and asthmatic. She had an extra reason for keeping her observations harmless and general: even her whispers were loud and liable to erupt like a malfunctioning barrel organ.

“I've _never_ been grasping, Jane,” she replied. “But I have six children living and three buried, and my husband had no fortune. The eldest, sitting over there, is only nineteen—you can judge for yourself. Always short of stock, and such difficult land. But if I've begged and prayed to anyone, it's been to God in heaven. Still, with one brother unmarried and the other childless after marrying twice, anyone might have thought!”

Meanwhile Mr. Vincy had looked at Mr. Rigg's impassive face, taken out his snuffbox, and tapped it. Then he put it away unopened. Snuff might clear the judgment, but the occasion hardly suited such an indulgence. “Perhaps Featherstone had kinder feelings than any of us allowed,” he whispered to his wife. “This funeral suggests he thought about everybody. It's a good sign when a man wants his friends to follow him, and isn't ashamed of them because they're humble. I'd be all the happier if he's left plenty of little legacies. They can be immensely useful to people with small means.”
“It's all been done as handsomely as possible—the crape, the silk, everything,” Mrs. Vincy said with satisfaction.

Fred, I regret to say, was having trouble suppressing laughter, which would have been still less appropriate than his father's snuffbox. He had overheard Jonah mention a “love-child.” With that suggestion in his mind, the stranger's face directly opposite seemed unbearably comic. Mary Garth noticed the twitching mouth and the refuge he took in coughing, and resourcefully rescued him by asking to exchange seats. This put him in a shadowy corner. Fred felt warmly disposed toward everyone, Rigg included. He was feeling especially charitable toward all these people, less fortunate than he knew himself to be, and would not for anything have misbehaved. Yet laughing was remarkably easy.

Everyone's attention shifted when the lawyer returned with the two brothers. The lawyer, Mr. Standish, had arrived at Stone Court that morning believing he knew exactly who would be pleased and who disappointed before the day ended. He expected to read the last of three wills he had prepared for Mr. Featherstone. Standish never adjusted his manner to his company. His deep-voiced, casual politeness was the same for everyone, as though he recognized no distinctions. His chief topics were the hay crop, which would be “very fine, by God!”; the latest reports on the King's health; and the Duke of Clarence, a sailor through and through and precisely the man to govern an island such as Britain.

Sitting before his fire, old Featherstone had often thought how surprised Standish would be one day. Certainly, if he had finally had his way and burned the will another lawyer had drawn up, he would have forfeited that minor satisfaction. But he had enjoyed turning it over in his mind. Mr. Standish was indeed surprised, though by no means sorry. On the contrary, discovering a second will gave his own curiosity a pleasant little stimulus, added to the prospect of watching the Featherstones' astonishment.

Solomon's and Jonah's feelings, meanwhile, hung in complete uncertainty. They imagined the earlier will must retain some force, and that poor Peter's earlier and later wishes might become so entangled that there would be endless “lawing” before anybody received his due. At least that inconvenience would be shared by all. They consequently came back with Mr. Standish wearing expressions of entirely neutral gravity. Solomon nevertheless brought out his white handkerchief again. Whatever happened, there would be touching passages; at funerals, even dry weeping was customarily presented in fine linen.

Perhaps Mary Garth's heart beat with the greatest excitement just then. She knew that it was effectively her doing that this second will had survived to be produced, and that it might profoundly change the lives of people in the room. Not another soul knew what had happened on that last night.

“The will now in my hand,” said Mr. Standish, seated at the table in the center of the room and taking his time over everything, including the coughs with which he prepared to clear his voice, “was prepared by me and signed by our late friend on August 9, 1825. I have, however, discovered a later document, previously unknown to me, dated July 20, 1826—less than a year afterward. In addition, I find”—his spectacled eyes moved carefully over the paper—“a codicil to this later will, dated March 1, 1828.”
“Dear me, dear me!” said sister Martha. She had not intended to be heard, but the accumulation of dates forced an utterance out of her.
“I shall read the earlier will first,” Mr. Standish continued, “as the deceased evidently intended, since he did not destroy it.”

The opening formalities seemed rather lengthy. Several people besides Solomon shook their heads sorrowfully, looking down. Everyone avoided everyone else's eyes. Most gazes rested on marks in the tablecloth or on Mr. Standish's bald head. Mary Garth was the exception. Since all the others were trying to look nowhere, she could safely watch them. At the first “give and bequeath,” she saw their complexions change almost imperceptibly, as though a faint tremor had passed through them. Only Mr. Rigg remained exactly as before. Indeed, with more urgent questions to consider, and the difficulty of listening to gifts that might or might not have been withdrawn, the company had forgotten him. Fred reddened. Mr. Vincy could no longer resist holding his snuffbox, although he kept it shut.

The smaller legacies came first. Even remembering that there was another will, in which poor Peter might have reconsidered, could not prevent mounting disgust and indignation. We like people to treat us well in every tense: past, present, and future. Yet five years ago Peter had been capable of leaving his own brothers and sisters only two hundred each, and his nephews and nieces a mere hundred. The Garths were not mentioned. Mrs. Vincy and Rosamond were to receive a hundred apiece. Mr. Trumbull got the gold-headed cane and fifty pounds. The other second cousins and the cousins present each received the same handsome sum—a sort of legacy, as the gloomy cousin observed, that got a man nowhere. More of this insulting trickle was directed toward absent people, doubtful connections who, one feared, were socially low. A quick reckoning suggested about three thousand had been distributed. Where was the rest meant to go? And the land? What had been revoked, and what remained? Had the changes improved matters or made them worse? Every feeling must be provisional and might prove inappropriate. The men could endure this muddled suspense in silence, some dropping their lower lips, others pursing them, as their facial habits dictated. Jane and Martha, overwhelmed by the questions, began to weep. Poor Mrs. Cranch was half comforted by the prospect of receiving any hundreds without working for them, and half aware how small her share was. Mrs. Waule could think of nothing but being his own sister and getting little, while someone else would get a great deal. Everyone now expected that great deal to go to Fred Vincy. Even the Vincys were astonished, however, to hear ten thousand pounds in named investments left to him. Would the land follow? Fred bit his lips to keep from smiling. Mrs. Vincy felt herself the happiest woman alive; in this dazzling prospect, the possibility of revocation dwindled out of sight.

Personal property still remained, besides the land. All of it went to one person, and that person was—O possibilities! O hopes built on the favor of secretive old gentlemen! O endless exclamations, still powerless to measure human folly!—the beneficiary of everything remaining was Joshua Rigg. He was also appointed sole executor and required henceforth to take the surname Featherstone.
A rustle passed around the room like a shiver. Every eye returned to Mr. Rigg, who showed no sign of astonishment.

“An extraordinary disposition of property!” cried Mr. Trumbull, for once preferring to be thought previously uninformed. “But another will exists—a further document. The deceased's final intentions have yet to be disclosed.”

Mary Garth knew that what they were about to hear did not express his final intentions. The second will canceled everything except the gifts to the socially humble people already mentioned—changes to some of these had occasioned the codicil—and the gift to Joshua Rigg of all the land in Lowick parish, together with the livestock and household furnishings. Everything else was to fund the building and endowment of homes for elderly men, to be called Featherstone's Alms-Houses. They were to stand on land near Middlemarch which the testator had already bought for that purpose. His wish, the document stated, was to please God Almighty. Nobody there received a farthing, though Mr. Trumbull retained the gold-headed cane. For a time the company seemed unable to speak. Mary did not dare look at Fred.

Mr. Vincy spoke first, after energetic use of his snuffbox. His indignation was loud. “The most inexplicable will I've ever heard! I'd say he wasn't in his right mind when he made it. I'd say this last will was invalid.” That word seemed to Mr. Vincy to put the matter in its proper light. “Wouldn't you, Standish?”

“I believe our late friend always understood what he was doing,” Mr. Standish replied. “Everything is entirely in order. A letter from Clemmens of Brassing is tied to the will. He prepared it—a thoroughly reputable solicitor.”

“I observed no mental derangement, no disturbance of the intellect, in the late Mr. Featherstone,” Borthrop Trumbull said. “But I consider this will eccentric. I was always happy to assist the old gentleman. He indicated distinctly enough that he felt an obligation which his will would acknowledge. As an acknowledgment of my services, the gold-headed cane is absurd. Fortunately, financial motives are beneath me.”
“I can't see anything particularly surprising,” said Caleb Garth. “A will such as you'd expect from an open, honest man would have been far more surprising. Personally, I wish wills didn't exist.”
“By God, that's an odd opinion for a Christian!” said the lawyer. “I'd like to hear how you defend that, Garth.”
“Well,” Caleb began, leaning forward, carefully arranging his fingertips and gazing thoughtfully at the floor. Words always seemed to him the most difficult part of business.

But Jonah Featherstone now made himself heard. “My brother Peter was always a first-rate hypocrite. This will beats everything, though. If I'd known, a wagon with six horses couldn't have dragged me away from Brassing. Tomorrow I'm wearing a white hat and a drab coat.”

“Dear me, dear me,” Mrs. Cranch sobbed. “And all the money we've spent on coming here, and that poor boy kept idle so long! It's the first I've heard of brother Peter being so eager to please God Almighty. If I were to be struck helpless for saying it, I'd still call it hard treatment. I can't think otherwise.”

“It won't help him where he's gone, I believe,” said Solomon. The bitterness was strikingly sincere, though his tone could not stop sounding sly. “Peter led a bad life. Almshouses won't conceal it, especially when he's had the nerve to reveal it at the end.”

“When all along he had a proper lawful family of his own—brothers, sisters, nephews, nieces—and sat with us at church whenever he chose to attend,” Mrs. Waule added. “He could have left his property so respectably, to people who've never gone in for extravagance or wild living of any sort, and aren't so poor they couldn't save every penny and increase it. And the trouble I've taken, coming here over and over to behave like a sister! All the while he had things on his conscience to make your flesh crawl. If the Almighty has permitted it, He means to punish him. Brother Solomon, I'm ready to go, if you'll drive me.”
“I've no wish ever to enter the place again,” Solomon replied. “I've land of my own, and property of my own to leave.”

“A sorry business, the way fortune deals with people,” said Jonah. “Having a little spirit never pays. Better to be a dog in the manger. Still, those of us above ground could take a lesson. One fool's will is quite enough for any family.”

“There are several ways to be a fool,” Solomon said. “I won't leave my money to be thrown down a drain, nor to foundlings from Africa. I prefer Featherstones born and bred, not people turned into Featherstones by having a name pasted on.”

Solomon delivered this loud aside to Mrs. Waule as he rose to leave with her. Jonah knew he could be far more cutting. But he reflected that insulting Stone Court's new owner served no purpose until it was certain he had no intention of welcoming witty men whose name he was about to share.

Joshua Rigg, in fact, seemed little concerned by insinuations. His manner did change markedly, however: he walked composedly up to Mr. Standish and began asking practical questions with complete assurance. His voice was high and chirping, his accent atrocious. Fred, no longer tempted to laugh at him, thought him the most vulgar monster he had ever encountered. Fred felt rather sick. The Middlemarch fabric merchant waited for a chance to speak to Mr. Rigg. Who could tell how many pairs of legs the new owner might need stockings for? Profit was more dependable than an inheritance. Besides, as only a second cousin, the merchant was detached enough to feel curious.

After his first outburst, Mr. Vincy had maintained a proud silence. Unpleasant thoughts absorbed him so completely that he did not think of leaving until he saw his wife beside Fred, holding her darling's hand and silently weeping. He got up immediately. Turning his back on the others, he murmured, “Steady, Lucy. Don't make yourself foolish in front of these people, my dear.” Then he added in his ordinary loud voice, “Order the phaeton, Fred. I haven't time to waste.”

Mary Garth had already been preparing to leave with her father. She met Fred in the hall and for the first time dared look at him. His face had the pinched pallor that sometimes comes over young faces, and the hand she shook was very cold. Mary was troubled too. She knew that, without intending it, she might have made a fatal difference to Fred's prospects.
“Goodbye,” she said, sadly and tenderly. “Have courage, Fred. I really believe you're better off without that money. What good did it do Mr. Featherstone?”

“That's easy enough to say,” Fred answered irritably. “What am I supposed to do? Now I'll have to enter the Church.” He knew this would annoy Mary; well, then she must suggest an alternative. “I'd expected to repay your father immediately and put everything right. And he hasn't left you even a hundred pounds. What will you do now, Mary?”
“Find another position, of course, as soon as possible. Father has enough to do supporting the others, without keeping me. Goodbye.”

Very soon Stone Court was empty of genuine, home-brewed Featherstones and its other familiar visitors. Another stranger had come to settle near Middlemarch. In Mr. Rigg Featherstone's case, however, people were more occupied with resenting the immediate, visible results than with speculating about his future influence. Nobody had enough prophetic insight to foresee what a trial of Joshua Rigg might bring to light.

At this point I am naturally drawn to consider how a low subject may be elevated. Historical parallels work remarkably well. Their chief disadvantage is that the conscientious narrator may lack space, or—which often amounts to the same thing—may be unable to recall any precisely, while remaining philosophically certain that, if known, they would illuminate the matter. A shorter, easier road to dignity might be this observation: no true story has ever existed that could not be told as a parable, with a monkey substituted for a margrave, or the reverse. Accordingly, everything I have narrated or shall narrate about humble people can be ennobled simply by treating it as a parable. Should bad habits and ugly consequences appear, the reader may take comfort in regarding their lack of refinement as merely figurative, and feel that he is effectively keeping quite fashionable company. Thus, even while I tell the truth about boors, my reader's imagination need not be wholly deprived of lords. And those petty sums on which a bankrupt of distinction would disdain to retire can be raised to the scale of great commercial transactions by the inexpensive addition of a proportionate number of zeros.

As for a provincial history whose participants all possess lofty moral standing, that must belong to a time considerably later than the first Reform Bill. Peter Featherstone, you will observe, was already dead and buried several months before Lord Grey took office.

chapters.title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXVI
paragraphs:
’T is strange to see the humors of these men,
These great aspiring spirits, that should be wise:
. . . . . . . .
For being the nature of great spirits to love
To be where they may be most eminent;
They, rating of themselves so farre above
Us in conceit, with whom they do frequent,
Imagine how we wonder and esteeme
All that they do or say; which makes them strive
To make our admiration more extreme,
Which they suppose they cannot, ’less they give
Notice of their extreme and highest thoughts.
—DANIEL: _Tragedy of Philotas_.

Mr. Vincy came home from hearing the will with his views on many subjects considerably altered. He was a man open to impressions, but inclined to express himself indirectly. A disappointing market for his silk braids made him swear at the groom; annoyance with his brother-in-law Bulstrode produced cutting observations on Methodism. His newly stern view of Fred's idleness now became apparent when he flung an embroidered cap out of the smoking room onto the hall floor.
“Well, sir,” he remarked as Fred headed for bed, “I hope you've decided to return next term and pass your examination. I've made up my mind, and I advise you not to waste time making up yours.”

Fred said nothing. He was too completely crushed. Twenty-four hours earlier, he had expected that by now he would no longer need to consider what to do: he would know that he need do nothing. He would hunt in a scarlet coat, own a first-rate hunter, ride to the meet on a fine hack, and earn general respect for it all. He would also repay Mr. Garth immediately, and Mary could have no further reason to refuse him. All this was supposed to happen without studying or any other inconvenience, through Providence's kindness as embodied in an old gentleman's whim. Now, at the end of those twenty-four hours, every confident expectation lay overturned. It seemed “rather hard lines” to be treated, while still smarting with disappointment, as though he could have prevented it. But he left without speaking, and his mother took his part.

“Don't treat the poor boy harshly, Vincy. He'll do well yet, although that wicked man deceived him. As surely as I'm sitting here, Fred will turn out well. Why else was he saved from the edge of the grave? I call it robbery. Promising him the land was as good as giving it. And what counts as a promise if making everybody believe you doesn't? Besides, he actually left him ten thousand pounds and then withdrew it.”
“Withdrew it!” Mr. Vincy repeated irritably. “The boy brings bad luck, Lucy, that's what I say. And you've always indulged him.”
“He was my first, Vincy. You made quite a fuss over him yourself when he arrived. Nobody could have been prouder,” said Mrs. Vincy, readily regaining her cheerful smile.
“Who can tell what a baby will grow into? No doubt I behaved like a fool,” her husband said, though his voice had softened.

“But whose children are handsomer or better than ours? Fred is miles ahead of other people's sons. You can hear in the way he speaks that he's mixed with university men. And where would you find another girl like Rosamond? Put her beside the grandest lady in the country and the comparison would only flatter her. Look at Mr. Lydgate. He's been everywhere and mixed with the best society, and he fell in love with her straightaway. Not that I wouldn't have preferred Rosamond to wait before getting engaged. On a visit she might have met someone who'd have been a much better match—I mean visiting her schoolfriend Miss Willoughby. That family has relations every bit as grand as Mr. Lydgate's.”
“Damn their relations!” exclaimed Mr. Vincy. “I've had my fill of relations. I don't want a son-in-law whose only recommendation is his family.”

“But, my dear,” Mrs. Vincy replied, “you seemed perfectly delighted. I wasn't home, admittedly, but Rosamond said you'd raised no objection whatever to the engagement. She's already started buying the finest linen and cambric for her underclothes.”

“Not with my approval,” said Mr. Vincy. “I've enough on my hands this year with an idle rascal for a son, without buying wedding clothes as well. Money couldn't be tighter; everyone's being ruined. I doubt Lydgate possesses a farthing. I won't consent to the wedding. They can wait, as their elders did before them.”
“Rosamond will be very upset, Vincy. You know you've never been able to bear refusing her.”
“Yes, I have. The sooner they break it off, the better. At this rate he'll never earn a living. All I hear of him making is enemies.”
“But Mr. Bulstrode thinks very highly of him, my dear. I'd expect the marriage to please _him_.”

“The devil it would!” said Mr. Vincy. “Bulstrode won't support them. If Lydgate imagines I'm providing money to set up their house, he's mistaken. That's all. I shall probably have to give up my horses soon. You'd better pass that on to Rosy.”

Mr. Vincy often followed this course: agree rashly in a jovial mood, then, on realizing his rashness, get someone else to perform the unpleasant retraction. Mrs. Vincy, never willingly opposing her husband, told Rosamond what he had said first thing next morning. Rosamond listened silently while examining some worked muslin. At the end she turned her graceful neck in a particular way which only long acquaintance would have taught you signified absolute obstinacy.
“What do you think, darling?” her mother asked with affectionate respect.

“Papa means no such thing,” Rosamond answered with complete composure. “He has always wanted me to marry the man I love. I intend to marry Mr. Lydgate. Papa gave his consent seven weeks ago. And I hope we'll take Mrs. Bretton's house.”

“Well, my dear, I'll leave your papa to you. You always manage everyone. But whenever we buy the damask, we must go to Sadler's—much better than Hopkins's. Mrs. Bretton's house is very big, though. I'd love you to have it, but furnishing it will be expensive: carpets and everything else, besides silver and glass. And you've heard your papa says he'll give no money. Do you suppose Mr. Lydgate is counting on any?”
“Surely you don't imagine I could ask him, Mamma. Naturally he knows his own circumstances.”

“He may have expected money, though, my dear. We all thought you'd receive a nice legacy too, besides Fred's. Now everything is so dreadful. There's no pleasure in thinking about anything, with that poor boy so disappointed.”

“That doesn't concern my marriage, Mamma. Fred needs to stop being idle. I'm taking this upstairs to Miss Morgan; she's very good at open hemming. Mary Garth could do some sewing for me now, I should think. Her needlework is exquisite—it's the nicest thing about her. I'd love double hems on all my cambric frills, and they take such a long time.”

Mrs. Vincy was right to trust Rosamond's ability to manage her father. For all his bluster, Mr. Vincy got his own way outside his dinners and his coursing about as rarely as a prime minister. Circumstances easily overpowered him, as they do most pleasure-loving, red-faced men. The circumstance called Rosamond was especially powerful, thanks to that gentle persistence which, as we know, lets a soft white living thing force its way through opposing rock. Papa was no rock. His only consistency lay in recurring changes of impulse, sometimes called habit. These gave him little chance of taking the one decisive course over his daughter's engagement: investigating Lydgate's finances thoroughly, declaring that he himself could provide no money, and forbidding either a hasty wedding or an engagement that would have to last too long. Written down, that sounds simple and easy. But an unpleasant resolution formed in the cold morning had as many enemies as an early frost and rarely survived the day's warming influences. Even Mr. Vincy's usual indirect but emphatic ways of expressing disapproval were much restricted here. Lydgate's pride made insinuations plainly dangerous, and throwing his hat on the floor was impossible. Mr. Vincy was slightly awed by him; slightly vain that he wanted Rosamond; slightly reluctant to discuss money, since his own position was weak; slightly afraid of losing an argument to a better-educated, better-bred man; and slightly afraid of displeasing his daughter. The role he preferred was generous host, beyond criticism. Business prevented any formal announcement of opposition during the first half of the day. Dinner, wine, whist, and general contentment prevented it during the second. Meanwhile each passing hour left its little deposit, gradually building the final reason for inaction: it was too late to act. The accepted suitor spent most evenings at Lowick Gate. Under Mr. Vincy's eyes, courtship flourished without depending in the least on advances from fathers-in-law or anticipated professional earnings. Young love spins such a delicate web!
